speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Canada was the

February 15, 1977
Home Insulation
strongest proponent of basket three incorporated in the final act of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe, popularly known as the Helsinki Agreement. As such we have reason to be concerned about what are regarded internationally as serious violations of the spirit and letter of that agreement by the Soviet Union. I refer in particular to the recent arrest of certain citizens of that country who have been endeavouring to ensure the full implementation of the Helsinki Agreement and who have been defending fundamental human rights whenever they are menaced in the Soviet Union or elsewhere.
From my own experience as foreign minister, I am aware of the difficulties and dangers of appearing to interfere in the internal affairs of another country. I am also aware of the implications of selecting particular individuals for mention. Since the signature of the Helsinki Agreement, however, such matters can no longer be regarded as purely internal, and there are occasions when specific protest is both justified and necessary, since failure to do so might imply indifference.
Accordingly, I seek leave to move under the provisions of Standing Order 43, seconded by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), and with support from all parties:
That the Secretary of State for External Affairs convey to the government of the Soviet Union the disappointment and deep concern of the elected representatives of the Canadian people in parliament assembled at the arrest of Alexander Ginsberg, Mykola Rundenko, Alexy Tikhy and Yuri Orlov.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-REVISIONS TO BANK ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked for the privilege of speaking to you and to the House at three o'clock as a result of the intervention of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) which I would be charitable in describing as an irresponsible intervention. In that intervention he seemed to imply that the failure of either a revision of the Bank Act or a reference of the white paper on banking to the committee was because of some difficulty which had occurred with regard to the official opposition. At least, I presume that that was the case, or perhaps it was the opposition in general.
I want to indicate to the hon. member that that is not so. As a matter of fact, when the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp) was the government House leader, I wrote to him on
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
August 26, 1976, asking for the reference of that white paper to the appropriate standing committee. I think it is important for the House to know that in my letter I said the following:
In recent months you and I have shared a common concern about the real relevance of the House of Commons to public policy decision-making. We both believe, I think, that the House is the ideal and proper point of contact between the people of Canada and their elected and appointed leaders. While this shared belief should lead over the next several months to worth-while reforms of our procedures, perhaps you might consider the following suggestion for a short-term experiment.
The next paragraph refers to Canadian banking legislation, and particularly the white paper. I go on to say this:
To this end I suggest that the white paper on Canadian banking legislation be referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs as soon as the House returns in October.
It is now February.
Hearings could be held before Bank Act amendments are drafted in their Final form and those institutions or individuals with an interest in the banking system could be heard. This seems to me to be preferable to a closed review of the report followed by the presentation to the House of a complex and essentially unchangeable draft bill.
This request was made of the then government House leader in August of 1976.
If the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs did hold hearings and issue a report, I assume that the committee stage of House deliberations on the actual amendments to the act would then be brief.
The summary to the white paper states on page 47: "The proposals in this white paper are based on the assumption that Canadians want a banking and Financial system which is national in scope, controlled by Canadians and as competitive as possible."
I conclude my letter by saying this:
I hope the House of Commons will be encouraged to find out what else Canadians expect from the banking system.
Subsequently I received a letter from the government House leader dated January 21, 1977. I believe I have referred to this already in the House. The letter is dated less than a month ago and there is a paragraph on page 2 which reads:
As you are aware, the Bank Act expires on June 30, 1977. We are making every effort to have a new bill ready for spring.
It has now become apparent from the answer that the new bill is merely to be a one-line bill extending the present banking system. The purpose of this intervention is to indicate that in the happy exchange of views which occurred-and which continues to occur-between the opposition and the government House leader there has been every hope, and every effort has been made by the official opposition, to have that white paper brought to the committee. I might say, without revealing any confidences at all, that this matter has been discussed between the present government House leader and myself. It was discussed on the basis that there was a willingness on the part of the present government House leader to have that paper come forward, but that I had to understand- which I did-that the discussion of that white paper might be interrupted by the presentation of a revision to the Bank Act.
I think we should be very clear that I have taken the view- and I know my predecessor took the same view-that the members of this House, not just on the opposition side but on the government side as well, have not had an opportunity to

This approach is not unique by any means, but it is innovative in terms of the day-to-day unfolding of parliament. So I want to make it clear to the House and to the hon. member for Ontario that in what he has said he has misled the House. I am sure it was inadvertent.

speechtext:
-I called a subcommittee meeting precisely to deal with questions relating to the white paper on banking and the proposed Bank Act which would be forthcoming. At that time, as chairman of the committee and with the consent of all members, I entered into negotiations with the government House leader and with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in an attempt to achieve agreement whereby this committee of the House would be given the white paper to study. The purpose of that directive of the subcommittee to me was so that we could begin public hearings on that working paper and therefore cut down the length of time which would be needed to debate the bill when it was brought forward. I discussed this matter with the government House leader and the Minister of Finance and agreement was reached whereby the white paper would be referred to our committee.

The agreement was reached on these conditions: first, that there would be a limited debate on the reference itself. I pursued the matter further and it was agreed with the government House leader and the Minister of Finance that the debate would be limited to no more than one day's duration, and that was quite acceptable. Second, the agreement was that the standing committee would complete its public hearings by Easter of this year, and following that we would move to clause by clause consideration of the bill, if it was before us by that time, and conclude by the end of this session.
The whole agreement broke down when I raised this question with the steering committee and with members of the Conservative party because the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who I presume was speaking for the members of his party, would not agree to a limited debate on the reference of the white paper. He indicated that the debate would last more than one day and in all likelihood that it would be a very extended debate. With that information brought forward by a representative of that party, I went back to the House leader and indicated that this was what was happening. That meant an end to the agreement, much to the chagrin of members of the New Democratic Party who wanted that reference, to members of this party who wanted the reference, to members of the government who were prepared to give the reference, and to some members of the hon. member's party who wanted to see a reference.
Those are the hard facts from my vantage point and my involvement in this matter. Therefore, the question that I raised and the comment that I made in that question is perfectly valid as far as I am concerned. Until the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton brought forward his communication with the House leader, I was not aware of it. The simple fact is that there appears to me to be a very legitimate misunderstanding between the House leader for the Conservatives and myself on this question and I-

and state their understanding of agreements that have taken place and negotiations that have taken place outside the chamber that by their very nature are not binding on this House. They ought not to be referred to, I think, and probably ought not to be referred to in a definitive way. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, you had notice that I intended to raise this matter of privilege which I suggest affects all of us. A Canadian Press story on the front page of today's Globe and Mail-which also was put out on the CBC radio news broadcasts-states that the Speaker of the National Assembly of Quebec "sits in gallery for foreigners". I suggest there are enough strains placed upon confederation these days without the need for pejorative and inaccurate headlines.

subtopic: MR. FAIRWEATHER-NEWSPAPER AND RADIO COMMENT ON NATIONAL ASSEMBLY OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. FAIRWEATHER-NEWSPAPER AND RADIO COMMENT ON NATIONAL ASSEMBLY OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
These headlines have already-I had in my notes that they are bound to jangle nerves already somewhat raw because of those who wish to dismantle this country. I do not mean to be preachy, but the gallery where Mr. Clement Richard sat yesterday is the Speaker's gallery where you, sir, extend your courtesy to a visitor whether it be the Speaker of the territorial government of the Northwest Territories, of Saskatchewan, of British Columbia, Venezuela or other countries outside Canada. It is my understanding that visitors of the Governor General, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), or Your Honour sit in that gallery when they are here.
A similarly phrased headline would not have followed, I suggest with great respect, a visit of the Speaker of the legislative assembly of my province, New Brunswick. I ask, why we are subjected to this type of headline in these days?

Mr. Speaker, I rise somewhat reluctantly on a point of order at this juncture. It deals with my question earlier in the question period. I know Your Honour has made an excellent interpretation of the questions and has discerned whether a representation has been made to any particular minister on any particular topic. I rise today because I feel very strongly about what I consider to be prima facie evidence of the infringement of the Bill of Rights of our country of the basic concepts and precepts of our common law principles of justice in Canada.
I want to bring to Your Honour's attention the fact that what I was attempting to do in the questions put to the Minister of National Revenue-and the Solicitor General, if he were here-was to bring the matter to their attention and request that they give an undertaking to stop this kind of activity with respect to legislation and acts under their particular jurisdiction. My purpose was to obtain, in the course of questioning, at least, an undertaking that they would review individually the applications to be made to the court with respect to this kind of application for writs of assistance in which there is no date of expiry, no specified officers or constables mentioned in the writ and which give unlimited powers to members of the national police.
It was not my intention to make a representation. I am sorry if I was not as clear as I might have been, but I feel so strongly about this question that I want to bring it to Your Honour's attention at this time so that I may pursue it at a subsequent time.

speechtext:
1. Under the Arrangement Regarding International Trade in Textiles, Canada maintained voluntary restraint arrangements with a number of major supplying countries to restrain the level of imports of certain textile products. Under these agreements, Canadian importers were free to purchase these textile products regardless of type or price from countries with whom Canada had restraint arrangements. 1.	What efforts has the government made to reunite 300 families in Canada separated from family members in Russia?
2.	If no progress is made in the near future, what alternatives are available to Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1. Since 1971, when Prime Minister Trudeau raised the question with Premier Kosygin of the Soviet Union, the Canadian Government has made a series of representations to the Soviet authorities in Ottawa and in Moscow on behalf of families in Canada separated from family members in the Soviet Union. Canada played a leading role in the preparation of the text on reunification of families which was incorporated in the final act of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe signed at Helsinki in August, 1975. Since then, representations to the Soviet government have been made at increasingly frequent intervals. Approaches were made by the Canadian ambassador in September and by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the Soviet foreign minister, Mr. Gromyko, during his visit to Moscow in October. Since then the question has again been discussed with the Soviet foreign ministry and the Soviet ambassador.
2. During the past year, some progress has been made in reuniting families with close relatives from the Soviet Union. While the pace in resolving cases on which we have made representations is slow, the Soviet authorities have in fact increased this year the total number of exit permits issued to people emigrating to join families in Canada. It is to be hoped that this progress will continue at an accelerated rate. The question of family reunification will be discussed at the CSCE follow-up meeting in Belgrade in 1977 when progress in implementing the final act will be reviewed in detail.

Air Pollution Studies Involving Environment Canada in New Brunswick since January 1, 1974; 1. Saint John Region Air Quality Study: This study was designed to follow up on the recommendations of the Lorneville Impact Study which assessed the effects upon air quality of the Coleson Cove Generating Station. It involves a monitoring network of six air quality stations and a program of computer modelling of atmospheric dispersion. It is hoped that the end result will be an aid to regional use planning and to the provincial air pollution control agencies. This study is being carried out in conjunction with Environment New Brunswick. 2. Air Pollution Assessment of Heating Plant at CFB Gagetown: Complaints have been received about emissions from this heading plant and a study is being carried out by a consultant under our supervision. 3. Air Pollution Study of Proposed Expanded N.B.E.P.C. Generating Station at Dalhousie, New Brunswick: This study was carried out at the request of the provincial department of the environment. Its purpose was to estimate ground level concentrations resulting from the proposed expansion of this generating station. The results were forwarded to the provincial department of the environment. The study involved computer modelling of dispersion from the stacks of the station. 4. Air Pollution Study in the Vicinity of the Lead Smelter at Belledune, N.B.: This study, also carried out at the request of the provincial government, involved computer modelling of dispersion of lead and particulates from the smelter. Much effort went into determining the emission rates at the smelter. At the present time the provincial government is carrying out an ambient air survey in the vicinity of Belledune, and the department is assisting them in the analysis of the samples that they are gathering. 5. Abatement Program, CIL Dalhousie Chlor-Alkali: This is not a study as such but is a program designed to ensure that the company is in compliance with the federal mercury emission limits to the air whose effect date is mid 1978. The department's activities there include inspections of the plant and meetings with plant personnel. 6. Lead-Free Gasoline Sampling: The department has an on-going program of sampling of lead-free gasoline in the Province of New Brunswick to ensure that federal regulations are met. The purpose of the regulation is to reduce emissions of lead from automobiles. 7. Leaded Gasoline Regulations:

The department takes quarterly samples from all refineries in New Brunswick to ensure that the leaded gasoline also meets the federal standards for leaded gasoline. Quarterly reports of lead usage are also compiled from the refineries. This is also intended to reduce emissions of lead to the atmosphere. 8. Evaluation, Inspection and Approval of DREE Funded Projects: This is an on-going activity whereby our department in co-operation with the New Brunswick Department of the Environment assesses the pollution aspects of DREE funded projects to ensure that they are not a cause of pollution. Funds are withheld until both federal and provincial agencies are satisfied. This aspect of the work involves much travel, inspection of installations, assessment of plans, etc. This activity is intended to prevent pollution from new sources. 9. EPS/AES Sulphate Monitoring Study-Eastern Canada: The purpose of this study which is just getting underway is to assess the importance of pollutants, primarily sulphates, heavy metals and nutrients, that may be transported over long distances, say from the Eastern Seaboard of the United States, and deposited here in the Maritimes. Some intensive monitoring was undertaken in August 1976 and it will be resumed by Environment Canada for a two year period beginning April 1, 1977.
There are other programs within DOE that are not specific to New Brunswick but which nevertheless are intended to alleviate air pollution there. These are as follows: 1. Development of Federal Air Emission Air Guidelines: Guidelines have been developped for the cement, asphalt and coke oven industries and others are being developed for the petroleum refining, pulp and paper ferrous foundries, non-ferrous foundries and iron and steel industries. These guidelines are available to the provincial air pollution agencies, including N.B. which they may adopt as regulations as they see fit. 2. Training of Provincial Personnel: DOE holds several courses a year in which provincial air pollution personnel are trained in the technology. 3. Training Operators of Federal Boilers and Incinerators with Respect to Air Pollution Control: The department intends to start this program this year in order to reduce air pollution from these installations. Training of operators in New Brunswick will be included.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF FEDERAL, PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL DEBT
speechtext:
That this House notes with distress the prodigious increase in the federal, provincial and municipal debt, which will result in the shattering of our country; and
That this House further regrets the fact that the Government has failed to advance any new formula for the financing of the public sector to correct this situation, for instance an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act allowing it to use the credit of the nation as currency in order to make long-term loans to the federal and provincial governments at an interest rate equivalent to administrative costs rather than the present six-month limit and to relieve the burden imposed on Canadians to repay up to five times the amount of the loans made to the various levels of government by banking institutions under the present system.
Mr. Speaker, it may be by a combination of circumstances that I can hardly understand, but very often on an opposition day allotted to the Social Credit Party of Canada, it is felt
February 15, 1977

necessary to rise on all kinds of questions of privilege, each more important than the other. I hope this is not done on purpose in order to shorten the time allotted to the motion before us today, but if it was deemed important to rise on the first question of privilege relating to the failure of the government to introduce a piece of legislation on banking, a review of or amendments to bank charters, I cannot but think that suddenly it is realized that some problems are really important and come to mind after someone else has laid them on paper.
Mr. Speaker, as years go by, problems seem to recur from generation to generation. After some years spent in parliament, our legislative responsibilities towards the Canadian people seem heavier and this has prompted me to consider in my remarks the merits of the so-called allotted days provided in the Standing Orders, days which may seem at times to be of minor interest. Still the members of the Social Credit Party of Canada believe that those days are quite important in the development of a democratic parliamentary system in Canada.
This is why each time we move a motion on an allotted day we always endeavour to tackle an issue of prime importance for the country, to draw the attention of the government on oversights or still to make constructive suggestions and exhort it to draft legislation aimed at improving our present systems in the financial, economic or social fields.
All those are problems that affect the whole population, and that is why we consider that those opposition days are very precious and ought to be used in such a way that they be profitable to the whole population, and that by the end of the day we could at least have made the cabinet aware of those problems. And then they could in turn during the next few months bring remedies to the problems we have detailed before parliament, to improve our fellow citizens' economic circumstances and thus make it possible for various federal, provincial and municipal administrations to better meet the needs of people under their jurisdiction. Therefore it is the exclusive privilege of the various opposition parties to choose the subject matter which will be debated in the House on those allotted days.
For many years, parliament was made up solely of members of the party in power and members of the opposition party: the old parties. Therefore it was then relatively easy for the opposition to have an understanding with the government on the distribution of allotted days for the Business of Supply as well as on the subject matter to be considered on such days. It was more or less a time for relaxation, for temporarily putting aside consideration of bills and for voicing some criticisms that the opposition deemed advisable to make. However, as time went on and in view of the behaviour of the old parties, Liberal and Progressive Conservative, who were as thick as thieves, some people lost confidence in them; this is how third parties were born.
That is why the people decided to elect officers who could convey ideas to parliament which in their view had value. As the result of the presence of third parties in the House
Governmental Debt
traditions as well as the old party behaviour did change somewhat. Parliament had to amend the allotted days, which are called opposition days. Needless to say, there has been a drastic change in allotted days since third parties came into being. One only has to refer to past years to realize that the allegation I just made is true and that the so-called official opposition must necessarily agree with the third parties by allocating the opposition days according to the number of seats held by the opposition parties in the parliament.
It is because of the events and circumstances I just enumerated that the Social Credit Party of Canada had the privilege of choosing the subject matter of today's motion which reads very clearly as follows:
-That this House notes with distress the prodigious increase in the federal, provincial and municipal debt, which will result in the shattering of our country;
What does that mean? Why do we say it will result in the shattering of our country? Because, Mr. Speaker, the federal and provincial governments hold conferences. To my knowledge, there have been 32 federal-provincial conferences in which I am interested as a Canadian, where they have discussed to know whether Ottawa will abandon some revenue sources to the benefit of the provinces and where the provinces have expressed their needs to Ottawa to get the required funds to meet their obligations. And the motion goes on:
That this House further regrets the fact that the Government has failed to advance any new formula for the financing of the public sector to correct this situation, for instance an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act allowing it to use the credit of the nation as currency in order to make long-term loans to the federal and provincial governments at an interest rate equivalent to administrative costs rather than the present six-month limit and to relieve the burden imposed on Canadians to repay up to five times-
-in interest-
-the amount of the loans made to the various levels of government by banking institutions under the present system.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in addition to being constructive criticism, the motion I am now sponsoring does make some practical suggestions and urges the government to bring forward amendments to an act which has been in force for almost 42 years, i.e. since March 11, 1935. Obviously, I will not have time to go over the whole debate that took place in the House of Commons when that act was passed. The debate started with a resolution presented on February 22, 1934, by the then minister of finance, Mr. Rose, who at that time told parliament that he would have to follow up with a bill to create a central bank in Canada. The then leader of the opposition, Mr. Mackenzie King-everybody knows at least his name-stated on February 22, 1934, as reported at pages 830 and 831 of Hansard, and I quote:	*
Liberalism believes that credit is a public matter, not of interest to bankers only, but of direct concern to the average citizen. It stands for the immediate establishment of a properly constituted national central bank, to perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issue, considered in terms of public need.
I repeat: .. . "considered in terms of public needs".
... A central bank is necessary to determine the supply of currency in relation to the domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people; and also to deal with the problems of international commerce and exchange.

February 15, 1977
Governmental Debt
That is precisely what we have been saying for years, but after 42 years, as intelligent people should be able to, it is time to make changes. The Bank of Canada fulfilled a tremendous task; the legislators of that time made no mistake when they decided to have that act passed by Parliament, but time has come to adapt its possibilities, its functions to modern needs, to the needs of today, because the act, as passed in 1934 under a Progressive Conservative government, says many things.
We say the same today, it is still true. The preamble of the act reads as follows:
Whereas it is desirable to establish a central bank in Canada to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation, to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment, so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and generally to promote the economic and financial welfare of the Dominion.
In those days, this country was still known as a dominion; but today, it is possible-I feel we would be justified in doing so-to write: to promote the economic and financial welfare of our country, Canada. That is what the motion requests: that the government go further, that it complete what the legislators of times gone envisaged; that is why we suggest that section 18(l)(i) be changed as suggested in the motion, because that section now reads as follows:
The Bank of Canada may
(i)	make loans or advances for periods not exceeding six months to the Government of Canada or the government of any province on the pledge or hypothecation of readily marketable securities issued or guaranteed by Canada or any province;
(j)	make loans to the Government of Canada or the government of any province, but such loans outstanding at any one time shall not, in the case of the Government of Canada, exceed one-third of the estimated revenue of such government for its fiscal year, and shall not in the case of any provincial government exceed one-fourth of such government's estimated revenue for its fiscal year; and such loans shall be repaid before the end of the first quarter after the end of the fiscal year of such government;
Mr. Speaker, this might have made sense at that time but in 1977 can you imagine a government which has to borrow let us say $150 million in order to close its financial year on March 31, being obliged to repay those $150 million sometime in June? How is it going to help? Well it will help temporarily but it will not solve the problem. For this reason we are suggesting that long term loans be granted by the Central Bank for the financing of the public sector in an orderly, intelligent way. Thus, people would have time to breathe before having to pay back, they could achieve something but at an interest rate just to cover operating, administrative and personnel expenses, in short all that is required in a well organized office, whereas today the government has only two ways of raising revenues to administer the country, like any provincial government: taxes and borrowings.
Some taxpayers are lending money to the government through savings, but the bulk of the loans are made to the federal government or the provinces by banking institutions under the present system, at very high interest rates, and those high interest rates paid by the government have some impact

on the private sector which must necessarily compete with the Federal government. In the end it creates inflation and the national debt is increasing at an alarming rate.
The same is true of provincial governments. Just to mention a few examples in support of my arguments, I shall draw your attention to the fact that our national debt which amounted to $30 billion in 1967 has increased to $57 billion in 1974. Over a seven year period, the national debt has increased by more than $25 billion. Was the federal government the only one faced with such an increase? No, according to the answer given by the then minister of finance (Mr. Turner) in the House, as recorded in Hansard on May 13, 1975, page 5737, where it is said that generally speaking the provincial debt has almost doubled.
For example, it is the case of Newfoundland where the debt has more than doubled, within six years, going from $584,000,000 in 1967 to $1,222,000,000 in 1973.
The province of Ontario, for example, which is considered a rich province, with the best administration in Canada, had in 1967, a gross debt of $5,561,000,000. Six years later it went up to $10,817,000,000 and is still rising. This debt pyramid within the present system inevitably brings about increased taxation, and taxes. This in turn fans inflation, which results in unemployment and unemployment, as an hon. member put it today to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) spells poverty. But at any rate, those were his words, not mine but I think that the way he put it was not that stupid.
What happens, Mr. Speaker, is this: the government is under an obligation to provide financial aid to the private sector which is crushed under a burden of interest to pay. One only has to look in the newspapers to see why there has been such a number of bankruptcies this year and yet in certain cases, the governments had given the industries substantial subsidies to help them set up businesses which would create jobs for workers.
I have only to quote as an example, Mr. Speaker, the case of Thetford Mines, in Quebec a riding which is represented by a member from the party of the majority, but not the party in power, because they have not got the power, as the power lays outside the House in the hands of money men who do not waste their time standing for parliament, as there is not much money to be made there. They look after their own interests but they they have servants inside the House, within Parliament. We have evidence of that. In any case, Mr. Speaker, in Thetford Mines the province of Quebec is buying back Bellevue products, a firm which went bankrupt.

I consider that when the federal government grants a loan to a provincial government, it is to enable that provincial government to provide services to the people, and neither the federal government, nor a provincial government with regard to a municipality, has any right to grant loans to make a profit. Responsible governments should not exist to make a profit, but to provide services to the people.
We should let private enterprise make loans to the same type of businesses for a profit; which is quite normal since there is room for competition in the private sector. But none of this should exist in the public sector, where it would damage the good relationship which must prevail in a federated Canada as we know it now. I believe that it is the duty of legislators to make the public aware of such transactions or loans, because they could create a debt for future generations who are not at all responsible for today's situation. Mr. Speaker, our remarks are more than just negative criticism. We have said so time and time again in the House, and we repeat it in the motion.
Governmental Debt
I am trying to explain it with my modest means to urge the government to set up a special committee of the House to make an in-depth study of that whole policy now in use in order that we may together bring in amendments to that Bank of Canada Act so it will be in a better position to serve not only the federal government but the provinces and, through the provinces, the municipalities.
How many members are now witnessing that certain municipalities incur expenditures for the construction of water and sewer facilities which are beyond the capacity to pay of local ratepayers, and those people have to bleed themselves white. The value of their property goes down because they have to pay nearly five times in interest the value of those facilities. That is what is bad. That is what Parliament must react against. And Parliament is the only authority in this country capable of setting things straight, ensuring justice in order to have a more just society, and it must act rapidly, efficiently and in a very orderly fashion.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I do hope that in the course of this day hon. members who will participate in this debate will follow my advice-you do not have to share my opinions but you have the duty to examine them, you have the duty to suggest better ones, if possible, and we will support them wholeheartedly. But what are we looking for? We are trying to improve the situation, and today's problem is one of dollars for the government of Ontario, the federal government, Quebec as well as all other provinces. It is a problem of revenue to meet our obligations.
Considering all the facts 1 just set forth with the best intentions in the world I do hope I will receive the very generous support of hon. members so we may all together convince the government to introduce the legislation we want to ensure proper Finance in this country. We must see that the authority of this Parliament is the real authority and that high finance just like our children in school complies with the legislation of this country whereas today it is governments that are submitted to the whims of high finance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer (Minister of Supply and Services):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF FEDERAL, PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL DEBT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many times has the Social Credit Party of Canada proposed similar amendments to our banking legislation. Indeed the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) will remember that he introduced a private bill on November 5, 1976 which was almost along the same lines as the motion he proposed to the House today. He also made similar proposals on October 22, 1974, on March 18, 1969 and on March 15, 1967.
Of course the government has considered the Social Credit proposals because at first glance they do seem to offer valid arguments likely to convince people they should readily and easily endorse that philosophy without seeing the consequences. That is why many times the government gave a clear and precise answer to arguments by raising counterproposals which must be weighed when they propose such sudden change in our monetary policies.

February 15, 1977
Governmental Debt
My first argument is of course that if the proposition were accepted, it would automatically fuel inflation, not only by the federal government but more particularly by the provincial and municipal governments. Why? Of course, when you can borrow money without interest, you are inclined to borrow more often, and fairly easily, without taking the consequences into account. Thus this could lead to a rapid increase in spending in the public sector. At the present time many Canadians have adopted the opposite thesis. They say that the public sector, either federal, provincial or local, accounts for a vast amount of Canadian outlays and that government expenditures should be limited. When you propose loans with nearly no interest, you invite the governments to make almost unlimited spending for a certain number of years at least.
Of course, the law allows the Bank of Canada to meet some of my hon. colleague's aspirations. Pursuant to sub-paragraphs 18(1 )i) and 18(l)j), it does not allow to lend funds to the provinces or to the federal government. But, pursuant to sub-paragraph 18(1 )c), the law allows the Bank of Canada to buy federal and provincial government bonds. Up to now, the Bank of Canada has bought only Canada saving bonds. Why? First because it has always felt, and rightly so, and the government has always adopted the same views, that it would amount to interfering in the finances of the provinces and, in some ways, it would have conflicts of interest in applying a responsible monetary policy.
In fact, if it were so allowed, the Bank of Canada would automatically be compelled to buy provincial governments bonds, it would be compelled to choose and, thus, to discriminate. The bank should have to study the financial situation of each province and territory to check whether the bonds were regularly issued, whether the interest rate is valid and if it should consider buying such bonds. The rates vary necessarily according to the provinces.
The provincial capacity for payments and redemptions varies too. In order to manage its portfolio in a responsible way, the bank should definitely not act according to the established percentages but should be very freely on the market, according to the economic situation. But this would be putting the bank in a particularly delicate situation on the political Field, I should say, because I suggest that the Bank of Canada should keep a certain leeway and a certain kind of freedom as far as the monetary policy of Canada is concerned.
A second point about the conflict of interest that would face the Bank of Canada. When we went through a period of monetary restraint and were faced with economic problems, the Bank of Canada might decide to sell some provincial or municipal bonds it was holding. The Bank of Canada would once again be in a conflict of interest situation because it would be in the position of having to take a decision of a generally political nature, namely which bonds should be put back on the market to restore some balance in the sound management of the monetary policy.

Well, what about federal bonds? The Bank of Canada buys Canada savings bonds. Is that not a conflict of interest situation? Is it not faced with a decision of an almost political nature in its policy of buying Canada savings bonds? In my view, that point cannot be made as far as the federal government is concerned. Anyway, the circumstances are not the same as in the case of provincial and municipal bonds. Because it is generally recognized that the federal government is responsible for Canada's monetary policy. Then government must cooperate with the Bank of Canada and ensure that the economy is managed in a responsible way.
Moreover, the provinces and the municipalities keep saying right and left that the federal government is responsible for Canada's economic stability. If this is true, and I believe it is, it means that the government must have the means to develop policies with the Bank of Canada and, of course, the monetary policy must go hand in hand with the fiscal policy drawn up by the government. This means that although the Bank of Canada may be in somewhat of a conflict of interest situation, although it would be facing choices of a very political nature as far as the provinces are concerned, that point cannot be made in relation to the Canadian government.
Mr. Speaker, there is a third point I should like to make to my collleagues in order to disprove their argument. To allow the Bank of Canada to make loans to the provinces without interest or with an interest that only covers the administration costs would be an indirect transfer of funds from the federal government to the provincial government, since the Bank of Canada is an instrument of the central government. Over the years, we have already accepted many fiscal and payment transfers to the provinces. We have already responded in a responsible way to the legitimate aspirations of the provinces which were asking for more funds to meet some of their obligations.
The great majority of payment transfers by the federal government to provincial governments have no string attached, which means the provinces are free to spend those moneys as they choose, without any obligation. However, it is true that some of the payments are made in keeping with federal-provincial agreements, so that the money must be used for very specific purposes but on the whole the money is transferred to the provinces without lien.
And what does the transfer of payments from the federal government to the provinces amount to? More than a fifth of the federal budget, more than a fifth of the taxes which are levied by the federal government is transferred automatically each year to the provinces. This needs to be emphasized, Mr. Speaker. The provinces do not have to levy taxes, they do not have to assume the often odious role of explaining to the people that they must levy taxes in order to get the money they need for their budgets. A fifth of the federal government's funds, a fifth of last year's $42 billion budget was transferred to the provinces, and even more, since some federal expenses go directly to aid the provincial and municipal governments.

Well, 1 think that the federal government is being very generous when it levies taxes on Canadians and transfers one fifth of the funds so generated to the provinces and, the same thing may be said about the provinces, when they give money to municipal governments to meet their needs. I think that all of us in this House, whether we are members of the opposition or of the majority parties, when we account for our budget and try to justify our expenses to the people, when we speak as members of the federal Parliament, we should stress the fact that a fifth of the taxes is actually levied on behalf of the provincial governments who do not have to assume the unpopular role of "saddling people with taxes."
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) referred to the federal public debt. He mentioned figures which look astonishing at first sight when we consider the growth of the Canadian public debt but I think such figures need explanations and should be placed in a general context. It is evident that the debt and the revenues are increasing, that government assets are growing and that the national gross product which represents goods and services produced in Canada is also expanding from year to years. But what does this growth mean, Mr. Speaker? I notice that I have caught the attention of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert). I believe it is important since he is the one who introduced the motion. But there are others who would like to rise and I presume they will have the opportunity to do so later on.
The gross national debt-the public debt as we call it- which is made up of the remaining non expired debt, that is outstanding federal bonds plus other debts which appear in the public accounts of Canada to pay employee pension funds for instance, is paid through the consolidated revenue fund. What was this debt in 1952? In 1952 it stood at $17 billion $17,257 billion to be exact-and in 1976 it amounted to $71,750 billion.
Mr. Speaker, what were the registered net assets of the federal government in 1952? They stood at $6,072 millions, and in 1976 at $48,454 millions. What does it mean? This means that the net debt was $11,185 millions in 1952, and $23,296 millions in 1976. What does it represent?
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us talk about the net debt as a percentage of the gross national product, that is the growth in Canada in terms of production of goods and services in our country.
In 1952, the net debt in regard to the gross national product amounted to 51 per cent. In 1976, this proportion has dropped to 14.5 per cent. This means that when we compare the gross national product, that is everything produced in Canada over a year, to the federal government's debt, we find that the figure reached 50 per cent in 1952 and has been now sharply reduced to 14 per cent. That is an important point to remember. This must necessarily be considered in the general context of Canadian economy; we should not be afraid of those figures, but rather consider the percentages they stand for.
Governmental Debt
From 1965 to 1976, the debt increased at a compound rate of 7 per cent where as within the same period, from 1965 to 1976, the NGP jumped from $61 billion to $190 billion, namely at a compound rate of 12 per cent. This means that our wealth increased faster than our debt, that we now have more assets than debts in Canada, and therefore that we are in a better financial position.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize that whenever the federal government borrows money, it borrows it on the Canadian market not on the American or foreign markets. We borrow through Canada Savings Bonds which are issued here, which means all our loans are Canadian loans and the majority of the payments on our loans, namely the interests, find their way back to the Canadian people. Historically, Canadians have always considered it a good thing to have Canada Savings Bonds in their wallets, in their safety boxes, because they are safe investments. And the hon. member for Bellechasse is perfectly aware of this, because he comes from the province of Quebec. Does anyone get nervous about Canada Savings Bonds? Not at all. Are there people who get nervous about the savings bonds issued by provincial governments? Yes, there are.
I could also take this opportunity to say something about the management of our monetary policy and the guidelines upon which are based the decisions and action of the Bank of Canada. Some 15 months ago, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Bouey, publicly stated for the first time the approximate limits within which the federal bank was trying to maintain the growth rate of monetary supply. Mr. Bouey had then added that the bracket aimed at should be progressively lowered during the years to come, so that our monetary policy could remain consistent with the national aim of a gradual reduction of the inflation rate, which is still a government priority, because as the hon. member knows, small wage-earners and small depositors as well as those who are defenceless when it comes to big unions or big companies are affected by those things.
Mr. Bouey indicated that the bank then wanted to maintain the annual growth of money and deposits computed at the medium rate of that aggregate for the three-month period ending on June 1975 or at a 10 per cent rate. Last fall, the bank announced that the minimum targets for the growth rate of money supply had been set at 8 and 12 per cent annually, such a rate to be calculated on the average level of a three-month period centered on March 1976. This announcement by the Bank of Canada about the reduction in the growth rate trend of the money supply was met with positive reactions. It was favourably received. Last summer, the growth rate trend of the money supply and demand deposits remained close to the lower level of the 8 to 12 per cent annual range aimed at by the Bank of Canada.
Accordingly, the Governor of the Bank of Canada announced on November 19, 1976, a reduction in the prime rate from 9'/i to 9 per cent. Mr. Bouey stated, and I quote:

February 15, 1977
Governmental Debt
This reduction in the prime rate is justified by the fact that Canada has been able in the last few months to control inflation better and to slow down the rate of monetary expansion.
Similar considerations led to the further reduction in the bank rate from 9 per cent to 8V2 per cent effective December 22, 1976, and to the most recent reduction from 8V2 per cent to 8 per cent effective February 1, 1977. These rate changes have led to a general easing of interest rates to businesses and consumers in Canada which will be an important support to steady economic growth in this country. These improvements in the financial environment are strong evidence to all Canadians of the benefits of a national program of restraint.
What these developments indicate is that the concerted action of the government in the fight against inflation continues to bear fruit. The actions of the Bank of Canada carry the full support of the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining in debate on the motion before us today, I think it is important to deal with it section by section. Hon. members will note that the motion starts out as follows:
That this House notes with distress the prodigious increase in the federal, provincial and municipal debt, which will result in the shattering of our country-
When we speak about "prodigious", I think we should refer to the Oxford dictionary, which says that the word means "marvellous, amazing, enormous, abnormal". If the mover of this motion is suggesting that the increase of our total debt in this country is "marvellous", I would not agree with him. If he says it is "amazing", I would agree in part. If he says it is "enormous", surely nobody in this House would disagree. If he says it is "abnormal", I would agree with him most heartily.
Before dealing more specifically with the first part of the motion, I should like to say that I find it most remarkable that in an age, in a month, in a year when we are faced with perhaps some of the most serious problems that have faced this nation since confederation, we should be confronted with a motion that when you read it in its entirety is simply harkening back to the tired, worn-out theories of social creditism. I say that because the Social Credit party that we have known in this country has from time to time espoused what is called the "funny money" theory. But basically I think it has been a Social Credit party of compassion. It was certainly a party that under its former leader, Mr. Caouette, at any given time showed great concern for unemployment and the well-being of the average Canadian. I would suggest that the Social Credit party, through the mover of this motion, could have given us a more challenging motion to consider in view of the tears that are taking place in the fabric of this fine country.
Perhaps it would be helpful to read into the record what some in the international economic world are saying about Canada today. For example, in a well respected publication,

the "Bank Credit Analyst", which puts out a special supplement called "Outlook, 1977", the economic conditions of various countries are dealt with. At page 41 it has the following to say about Canada:
So you can see the basic ingredients of financial disaster in Canada-an overvalued currency sustained only by continuous recourse on a vast scale to foreign credit, huge budget deficits and balance of payments deficits, an uncontrollable public sector, sharply declining competitive position of manufacturing and a persistent shift of employment to unproductive "overhead" areas and away from the producing sectors. Corporate profits and the rate of return on capital have been sharply eroded as a result of this process and, more recently, by the controls program. Investment in goods-producing industries is falling at a rate which, if continued, will threaten the long-term viability of the economy. Private capital inflows for investment have slowed dramatically, partly due to the hostile political climate, controls on foreign investment and punitive taxation, and the outflow of private capital is on an accelerating trend.
It doesn't take much imagination to see where things are heading. As you would expect, the economic recovery of the past 18 months has been of very poor quality, supported primarily by government spending and deficits, subsidies to the housing industry, wage inflation and a temporary lift in exports due to some inventory restocking in the U.S. and elsewhere.
Unemployment is very high and could go much higher on existing policies.
Mr. Speaker, in total, 12 separate points of concern are spelled out in those two paragraphs. In short, this country is in trouble economically. I think it is time the government and all members of the House addressed themselves to the simple question: Why, with the potential we have in Canada, are we getting into the type of trouble we are now living with?
I listened with some interest to the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) because I hoped he would tell us that they planned to change their ways. I notice that he dwelt very gently on the question of credit. He pointed out that he felt if we became party to the Social Credit type of philosophy, somehow it would be inflationary. He pointed out, too, why he felt it would be inflationary. He dealt with the municipal level and the provincial level. Strangely enough, when he came to the federal level he said, "These rules do not apply. The relationship we have to the Bank of Canada is, somehow or other, unique. The relationship is one where, if we wish to bring monetary stances into line with fiscal stances, that is our prerogative."
That, perhaps, is the apex of the main problem in Canada today-the attitude on the part of the ministry that has been running this country since 1968. In short, they have chosen to use our monetary and fiscal position in Canada to suit their own political expediency instead of meeting the economic realities of the day. When I say that, I say it very advisedly. Let us not forget the simple fact that there is absolutely no mystery about where inflation comes from in any country. In Canada, inflation is manufactured in Ottawa: inflation is manufactured by the government of the day, namely, the Trudeau government.

speechtext:
Over the last 24 or 25 years it is interesting to review, on one hand, what has been the inflationary stance in Canada and, on the other hand, what has been the real growth and the growth in our monetary system through those four six-year periods. One need not be a scholar of economics to
February 15, 1977

know exactly what has happened. Incidentally, I am relying on government figures tabled in this House in response to a question I placed on the order paper on October 21 last. In the six years ending October, 1958, the rate of inflation in Canada was 8.6 per cent. I emphasize those figures-in those six years our inflation rate was 8.6 per cent. For the next six years ending in October, 1964, our inflation rate went down to 7.6 per cent. But in the next six years it rose to 24.1 per cent, and in the last six years ending October, 1976, the inflation rate in this country was 55.3 per cent. In short, our inflation rate escalated from 8.6 per cent and 7.6 per cent in the first two six-year periods to which I referred, to a rate of 55.3 per cent in the last six years.
Consider the increased money supply which has been generated in our economy. We find that in the first six years referred to our money supply rose by 25.9 per cent compared with real growth of 22.8 per cent. In short, we then witnessed better management of our fiscal and monetary matters. The money supply increased at approximately the same rate as the real growth in the economy. I point out that those low inflation years were basically Conservative government years. In those years the money supply went up 19.9 per cent, but the real growth of the economy was 31.6 per cent. Clearly, one could not call the increase in the money supply in those years an inflationary increase.
However, in the next six-year period we note a shift in conformity with Liberal philosophy. For the first time, the increase in the money supply started to overtake the real growth in the economy. We find that in that six-year period the money supply rose by 43.2 per cent while in real terms the economy grew by only 34.7 per cent. It is also interesting to note what happened to our money supply in the period October, 1970, to October, 1976. Mr. Speaker, it grew by 100.2 per cent while in real terms the economy grew by 31.7 per cent. Is it any wonder that this nation has experienced a 55.3 per cent rate of inflation when you consider that in the period when the real growth in the economy was 31.7 per cent the government expanded the money supply by 100.2 per cent?
Let us look at the matter in another way to see to what extent the government has overinflated the money system. We find that whereas the growth of the money supply approximately equalled the real growth of the economy in the six years ending in 1964, the period when inflation had been running at only 7.6 per cent, the growth of the money supply in the next period alluded to, because the government overcreated money, or printed it as some might say, rose five-fold as compared with the real growth of the economy. Those are the facts.
The minister generalized about the inflationary impact of the Social Credit philosophy and proposal. I can only say that the minister should have done some homework. Essentially, his government has adopted many of the principles advocated by the Social Credit party, nameiy, the monetization of the tremendous debt this government has incurred since assuming
Governmental Debt
power in 1968. Let me be specific. The government likes to waffle, to obscure the real size of this debt. We heard certain figures mentioned today. According to the answer to my question on the order paper, the gross national debt in Canada as of March 31, 1975, including contingent liabilities-I emphasize these contingency liabilities because the government loves to minimize its debt by not including them-was $78,326 billion. That was two years ago. By this time it is more than likely that that debt exceeds $80 billion-probably $90 billion if all contingencies are taken into accounts. I point out that when the government took power in March, 1968, the gross debt in Canada was only $42 billion. Clearly, since gaining power the government has more than doubled this debt.
The point I wish to make is that when a government spends and overspends to the extent this government has been doing, it can cover its spending only in three ways. It can do the honourable thing and tax in order to cover its outgoing expenditures or it can borrow funds from the private sector. If it borrows too much from the private sector, it will drive up interest rates in that sector. Third, the government can do the most dishonourable thing and monetize its debt by falling back on the Bank of Canada. To a large extent, the government has followed the last of these courses in financing the debts to which I have referred.
Check my figures, Mr. Speaker. Everyone in the Bank of Canada brings out a statement on the fiscal position of Canada. Included in that statement is a breakdown of the total financial needs of Canada. The bank shows where the government has raised money. I have referred to the six-year period ending in 1970. It is interesting to note that while our inflation rate was rising somewhat, the government was still borrowing moderate amounts from the Bank of Canada to finance the ongoing operations of government. In that six-year period total government borrowings from the Bank of Canada amounted to $1,163 billion.
Then we saw a change of heart on the government benches. Perhaps that change of heart became most obvious when John Turner took over as minister of finance. Of all the finance ministers who have reigned in Canada since confederation, there was never a spender to equal John Turner when he was minister of finance.

the last six years this government has monetized $4,159 million of debt alone. Why is all this significant? It is significant because that debt is one of the main instruments for increasing the M-1 supply, the basic money supply in this country, and if the money supply is increased at a rate faster than the real growth in the economy, the result is inflation; there can be no doubt about it.
The government may pretend it does not know how to control inflation. It can state, as it did, that we needed wage and price controls to control inflation. It can state that the labour unions are the bad boys, or that businessmen are causing inflation. The truth is that the government itself has caused inflation-and the Canadian public must never be allowed to forget it. The creation of extra money supplies, together with an overly expanding fiscal stance, has led to the inflation now afflicting this country. The Minister of Supply and Services gave a nodding acceptance to this in his speech.

speechtext:
He tried cleverly to pass the blame to the provinces and municipalities. But we find that the provinces are controlling their spending. They are controlling their spending increases more effectively than the federal government. That is exactly the reverse of what should be happening. If we want to get a handle on inflation, it is absolutely essential that we first accept the proposition that we must lower the federal government's take of the gross national product at a faster rate than has been taking place. When I speak about growth in federal government spending, I emphasize that between 1967 and 1977 Ottawa will increase their spending by 289.3 per cent, or an average of 14.7 per cent per year. In 1967, the total budget was $9,867 million. In 1977, it is $38,417 million. If we exclude defence, which has been growing much slower than other expenditures at the federal level, we find that federal spending has gone up 362.8 per cent, or an average of 15.8 per cent per year over the past ten years.
The motion is relevant in this sense. If it is used as a focal point to highlight why we have inflation in this country, to highlight that this government has thrust us into more debt per capita than ever before-and unfortunately they not only thrust us into debt but they have monetized the high proportion of that debt with the Bank of Canada, which in turn has given us inflation-it will be useful.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF FEDERAL, PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL DEBT
speechtext:
Last night was a very interesting thing to observe. When the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) was speaking, a number of members of the Social Credit party were in the chamber. I could see they were listening. They did not agree with everything the hon. member for Nickel Belt was saying. However, their instincts, their feelings for the little man and their sense that our tax system is oppressive and weighs heavily on the little man, favouring the big man, are the same as ours. That is quite clear, and I respect that.
Whatever the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) had to say about the theories put forward by the Social Credit party-and the same holds true for the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens)-what they have is for more important than the facile sophistication of the two spokesmen for the respective parties. They have an instinct for the truth. The great geniuses of the Liberal and Conservative parties have had the opportunity to govern, or misgovern, this country at one time or another. They think they know what they are doing. They say to the Social Credit party that they have a very unsophisticated theory, that they do not understand how the whole system works, and then gently try to explain how it does work.
They know something that the people in my party know. We have a society where people have needs. We have productive resources that are sitting idle. We have people who need houses, people who need jobs, all the capital you could want, and all the resources one could possibly hope for. We have so much food that we do not know what to do with it. In fact, the farmers are encouraged not to grow more crops. How can you have all these things and say you cannot put them together?
The hon. member for York-Simcoe says that the villain is the money supply, that the Liberals are in fact Social Credit-ers and that they have been responsible for increasing the money supply. That accusation has some truth. In 1963 the Liberals, under Walter Gordon who went on to be minister of finance, supported in a very strong way a Social Credit motion to change the whole economy. The Liberals supported it. That is the way they are. They woo you one day, and leave you the next. They are very unfaithful lovers. "Kiss them and leave them"-that is their attitude.
The germ of what is being said in Social Credit theory is true. It is the same germ that is contained in Keynesian economics. The problem with our society today is that we do not have purchasing power where it is needed. In other words, those who need houses and have other needs do not have the money with which to buy them. Something is wrong with the system. I am not going to say that the A plus B theory of Major Douglas explains it in an adequate way, because I would not presume to understand it. I was a little confused, especially when it was translated from the French.
We have to find some way of increasing purchasing power in our society. There are one million people unemployed. What went wrong with our geniuses? What went wrong with our
February 15, 1977

sophisticated people who hold degrees from every university in the universe? We have inflation at the same time as we have one million people unemployed. That is something to which these people must address themselves.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe pointed the finger at the Liberal party. He said it is their fault. His party did not behave any differently when they were in office. I am sorry 1 do not have the figures on the money supply when the Conservatives held office. However, they had to throw out the governor of the Bank of Canada because he would not increase the money supply fast enough. How can you hold the money supply responsible for everything that goes on? It is as though the price of oil did not increase 400 per cent and the prices of commodities did not rise. Most causes of inflation of the past few years can be attributed to everything but the money supply. The money supply had to be generated in order to pay the higher costs involved. The government and the official opposition continually harp that the money supply is always the villain; that if you increase purchasing power, you wreck society. That is just not so. They have not increased purchasing power or the money supply during the last year. Have they really helped the employment situation? Are people going back to work because the money supply has not been increased? The situation is worse than ever. The hon. member for York-Simcoe often argues that we have to increase investment. We have increased investment over and over again, with no effect. Very often when you increase investment you throw more people out of work. Therefore, the problem cannot be resolved by increasing investment. We have idle plant capacity, with less than 82 per cent employed. For what purpose do you increase investment?
Through the tax bill the government increased the ability of high-income people to save. There are some reasons for objecting to that. The effect of allowing people in higher income tax brackets to get this kind of benefit is that the very people who need the purchasing power and would use it to get the economy in action have to pay higher taxes. There is no such thing as tax avoidance to the extent that one group of people can shelter their tax and another group has to make it up. If you provide benefits which are essentially of greatest benefit to those in higher income brackets, it means that people in lower income brackets have to make it up in one way or another. They will do it through sales taxes; they will do it through income taxes; they will do it through taxes which might have been reduced but were not reduced. But the point is that it has to be made up at some point.
There is no way out of the morass we are in at the present time except to increase purchasing power for those at the lower end of the income scale. We have reached a kind of plateau, Mr. Speaker, in our society. Not only our society, but western society in general, I think, is in serious trouble. If you take a look around you will find that people in the middle and upper income brackets are accumulating savings at the greatest rate in history. There is no shortage of savings. We may, in fact, be reaching a point where the saturation of goods is such that
Governmental Debt
people in upper and middle income brackets really do not need to buy anything any more; they already possess most of the things they want. If you are going to increase purchases, if you are to keep the wheels rolling-aside from the moral aspect of income distribution, and aside from the justice aspect of income redistribution-you have to find a way to increase the purchasing power of those at the lowest end of the economic scale, or you will never get people back to work.
You can see a phenomenal amount of savings being made available to people in the middle and upper income tax brackets, and how they are rushing to put it away. Normally, one could say that savings are a good thing, and I think that generally savings are a good thing. But it is also possible for what might be a virtue in terms of individual savings to be a collective disaster if a whole nation does it instead of redistributing that income in some way so as to provide full employment for the nation. That is really what is being talked about in a motion of the kind before us. We might argue about techniques, about whether you are going to have interest-free money or not, but the germ of an idea is there and it has never been answered.
People have laughed at the Social Credit movement for a long time, particularly those sophisticates in the Liberal and Conservative parties. When I listened to the minister and to the official spokesman for the Conservative party, I thought they were getting ready for the next Quebec election. They sounded as if they were going into the Creditiste strongholds and those were the arguments they were going to use against the Creditistes. In other words, "Don't vote for these guys; they don't know what they are talking about. Vote for us; we know how to run the economy; we know how to give you one million unemployed. Don't listen to those guys." They are already sharpening up for the next federal election. But that idea stays alive.
I think there is a lot wrong with the Social Credit theory, but I do not have time to go into the negative aspects of it today. There is a lot wrong with it, or obviously I would be a Social Crediter. I think there are problems with it. But one thing nobody has been able to answer is why this idea stays alive. If it were patently false, if it were indefensible, surely the people who voted Social Credit or for the Creditistes in Quebec would have rejected them. They are not foolish people. But I think that despite the fact they do not have degrees in economics, either the people who run for the Social Credit party or who vote for them, their instincts tell them there is something wrong with the sophisticated theories put out by the old-line parties. So nobody has been able to answer that great paradox: Poverty in the midst of plenty, and unemployment when there is so much to be done. It is to that paradox that the motion addresses itself, and in that respect the viewpoints put forward in this motion deserve respect and attention.
