speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the very clear statement made by my colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
February 15, 1977
Governmental Debt
Lambert), I do not intend to dwell on the means which the government should now be taking to control the staggering rise of our national debt which will lead this country directly to disaster.
I would like to discuss for a brief moment our public financing system, mainly since Confederation and thus note its disastrous effects on our Canadian community.
When we examine the public financing system in Canada and try to detect its shortcomings and bring about improvements in accordance with the wishes of all the provinces of Canada, we are aware of the faulty distribution of taxation powers which has been the source of our worst struggles since Confederation in 1867.
This little historical review will enable us to pinpoint the primary cause, I was going to say, the main cause of all our internal wranglings. Our problem is nothing else but a money problem, a dollars and cents problem. Matters of language, religion and even races are futile compared to our financial problems which result in the deepest indebtedness, as it becomes financially impossible to reimburse the capital because the interests must be paid five times before a dollar of capital can be reimbursed. Mr. Speaker, there are several ways of subduing a nation: militarily, politically or otherwise, but the most hateful is to subdue it financially. God knows to what extent the central government has taken advantage of this in the last hundred years to restrain financially the influence of the provinces in fields coming under their exclusive jurisdiction.
I wonder, after reviewing the events of the last hundred years, if that diabolical bond was not dreamed up by the British government which had absolute control over that North American colony known as Canada, because the British were well aware of the motto: divide and rule. The primary concern was to safeguard the interests of the Crown in the face of British subjects, although by means that were not always civilized. For that reason, I am of those who believe that the British North America Act was first and foremost a political gesture on the part of the government in London which, through a simple private bill sponsored by the Ministry of Colonization, foisted upon its subjects of the northern colony a sham responsible government which it called the new Confederation of British North America.
We find here that the British Crown acted very diplomatically, since it was essential to prevent an armed conflict between the English and the French who were then in greater numbers. The Crown knew full well that while the federal government and the provinces would be fighting over the biggest slice of the cake, its interests, which were to collect as much as it could in taxes from Canada, would be served. It is somewhat like the manager of two big boxers. He will have them fight together better to exploit them. I think that is what the Canadians destined to live together in Canada on that American soil, Anglophones and Francophones alike, never did understand very well. Still, we seem to be sensible people, on

both sides. Why not sit down once and for all around a table and discuss sensibly the whole matter of money and indebtedness. That, in short, is the main sidelight of our financial history and the cause of our perpetual conflicts.
What does the federal government do? What does it want? More money and more ways of getting the provinces into debt. What about the provinces? What do they want? More money and more borrowing powers to meet the needs of the municipalities. Look at our cities municipalities, and school boards: they also need money. The problem cannot be solved at the bottom of the pyramid, that is, by the Canadian people, the powerless victims of that financial drama. Our society is sick. The central government is power hungry. It wants to be the unchallenged master of Canada and to achieve that status it will resort to every means at its disposal. On the one hand, it proclaims ministerial decrees from the heights of its authority, foisting this or that law or guideline upon the provinces. On the other hand, like a snake, it worms its way into exclusively provincial jurisdiction, under the pretext of helping, like the thief who distributes his spoils provided he reaps some popularity.
The federal government acts as if the provinces did not have enough intelligent men to manage its affairs and reach agreements among themselves. Just a few years ago, the government even set up a department to return to the provinces some of the funds collected in those same provinces without going through their governments. In years past, it invented the infamous shared-cost programs, of which there were 49 in 1964 and perhaps even more today.
Since the very beginning, Quebec has always asked to opt out of programs within its jurisdiction and to get tax points in return, because all the central government does it to collect taxes on behalf of the provinces and to give them back some of this money. I say some of this money because once, when I asked in the House what percentage was given back to the provinces, I was told that $2 out of every $5 collected was returned to the provinces. We heard quite a different story this afternoon, and I shall return to it later.
Ever since then, I have given my full support to the province of Quebec in the matter of tax patriation because it is really too costly to have the taxes collected by the federal government. More recently, the government created the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, supposedly to fight against regional disparity. This objective is good in itself, but what it hides is not so good. I still remember a meeting of the Committee on Regional Economic Expansion when we were asked to vote $500 million just before a general election. The then minister, the hon. Jean Marchand, hurried through the regions handing out millions of dollars, especially to industries with Liberal tendencies, which later went bankrupt or sold out after having pocketed millions of DREE dollars. Most industries that went bankrupt had probably forgotten that the subsidies they were given did not even cover the interest on the loans they required.
However, this was not the important thing for the Liberal party since the political objectives of the election campaign
February 15, 1977

had been attained. It is the same today: You only have to watch the forthcoming by-elections. Just watch the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) at work; he has already proven himself. He will be called upon to visit various constitutencies where he will distribute his generous gifts as in past years and past elections in an attempt to sweeten up the people. Just watch him. The other ministers and not only the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion will do this; in the last election, 12 ministers came to my constituency. Just watch them and tell me after the by-elections.
1 hope that the people in Quebec will continue to keep their eyes and ears open. All these subsidies only increase the debt of the public sector, that is the provinces, the cities and the municipalities. When a subsidy is promised, it generally covers only the interests on the loan needed by the parish or the city. We have the proof of this today in our region, in my riding, where the interests-I looked at the budget myself-on the debts resulting from these grants or loan promises, the interests alone represent 50 per cent of the total budget of the cities or municipalities. Is it not hypocrisy to get a municipality into debt and then use it to play politics? How can you hope to pay off the capital at those interest rates? And all this is an attempt to win an impossible political victory, since the more they put into my riding, the more they lost! The only purpose is probably to distract the provinces' attention or take their minds off their problems.
The federal government convenes federal-provincial conferences to impose its will on the provinces. From the early days of the Confederation pact, I always call it "confederative package", we have always found the same themes, the same wrangling over the separation of powers, for ever increasing taxes, more indebtness. Such reports make very tedious and irritating reading because several provinces, and Quebec in particular, are getting fed up with federal dictatorship and with the Trudeau administration and his strong central government.
We are convinced that the only way to restore some hope for unity in Canada is to start giving back the provinces their own jurisdictions and taxation powers commensurate with their obligations prior to all bargaining, full authority on taxation matters should be returned to the provinces. Even though the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) keeps telling the Quebec people to hold the referendum as soon as possible and that he, the Prime Minister, would start writing a new constitution if necessary, whereas the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) threatens to send the army in should Quebec proclaim its independence, preferring such threats and utterances will be to no avail because the Quebec people are no longer nervous. There is only one thing, which can serve any purpose and which incidentally, may be instrumental in bringing Quebec back to the bargaining table that is if the federal government gives back to Quebec the whole balance of taxation rights which it has claiming for a 100 years; let the federal government get out of areas which are under exclusive provincial jurisdiction, such as health, education, culture, language
Governmental Debt
and so on; let the central government stop granting loans carrying an 11 per cent interest rate to provinces, which have to pay back fivefold the small amounts which were lent to them.
The Liberals will contend they are doing what they do to help the province of Quebec! The best way to help the people of Quebec at this stage is to be honest for once in a hundred years, and give them back what is rightfully theirs and restore the rights of the provincial government so that it can carry out its responsibilities. In other words, let the thief out of the Quebec family home, and peace will return. The things we are asking for today are not new, Mr. Speaker. Others long before us have done so for the provinces to reduce their debt. Besides, we find that the first province which used direct taxation was British Columbia when they taxed individual income.
Later, the province of Quebec began to tax corporate income. I think the government was not interested then in direct taxation, because it produced almost nothing. They kept for themselves customs fees and other more profitable indirect levies. But as soon as the federal government realized that they could get large sums of money from direct taxation, they decided to get into this field, and for this they always took the opportunity of a war, since they had to find an excuse to invade this area of taxation.
The first time, it was during the war of 1914, when they took hold of a large part of direct taxation, and with the war of 1939, more precisely in 1942, the King administration hypocritically urged the provinces to relinquish all provincial direct taxation fields. The opportunity was excellent, too good to miss, and so Ottawa took over for five years.
Ever since 1867, the provinces keep claiming from the central government either the abandonment of joint programs or the recovery of their rights.
And we have handfuls of newspapers. For example, I have here a newspaper dated January 13, 1964 in which the hon. member Maurice Lamontagne is reported as saying:
Possible abandonment by Ottawa of joint programs.
And a Social Crediter he was not.
Then I quote from a newspaper of 1964:
Quebec plans to withdraw from 7 of the 49 joint programs.
And so it goes. From another Quebec newspaper of 1964, I quote:
Quebec must at any cost recover its fiscal rights.
At next week's federal-provincial conference, the Quebec government will reiterate its request for 100 per cent of the direct taxes collected by Ottawa in this province.
Mr. Speaker, those are the arguments we hear not only from Quebec but from the other provinces wishing to recover their rights. As you can see, all prime ministers, one after the other, pressed for those rights. Is it any wonder then that the new Quebec government does not trust this government any longer? First of all, we have to comply with joint agreements, and bring this government to its senses if we want Canada to survive. We are faced with the worst bureaucratic and financial dictatorship this country has ever known since Confedera-
February 15, 1977

Governmental Debt
tion. We have to restore democracy and ensure absolute self-reliance and respect for provincial jurisdictions, if we want Quebec to resume discussions with federal authorities.
As far as the Bank of Canada is concerned, the minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) surprised everyone of us today by saying he could not monetize the nation's credit because it would be inflationary. But, Mr. Speaker, can you imagine how surprised I was, since I have always thought inflation was due to too high a rate of interest. The cause of inflation is excessive bank interest and discount rates by the Bank of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate since it provides one with an opportunity to place on the record some
February 15, 1977

of the gross failures of this government in dealing with the economic concerns and realities of this country, and also to place on the record some of the gross inadequacies in its management of public funds. I think the hon. member who preceded me outlined the philosophy which governs this government. It is guided more by politics than by anything which would resemble sound business principles. Some of the things which have been going on in the province of Quebec in the government's quest to win a few by-elections is probably indicative of the fact that it would do anything for political partisan gain. In many respects this attributes in large part to the problem alluded to in this motion, namely, the abnormal increase in the size of the debt of all levels of government.
I must say at the outset that my first observation is that in terms of size and power, the federal government has to accept the major portion of the blame for the massive debt which has accumulated in this country. There can be no doubt about that. My friends the members of the Social Credit party have proposed a solution and a philosophy which they feel would work toward ameliorating and dealing with that particular problem. I am not going to comment too much on that particular aspect, but I want to talk about the accrual of this significant debt which costs Canadian taxpayers millions and millions of dollars to service year in and year out.
Last year Canada was the top borrower in the international marketplace; it borrowed $9.2 billion. In all, Canada absorbed about 16 per cent of the total funds borrowed on world capital markets. The next largest borrowing nation was Brazil, which borrowed $3.4 billion. The great majority of this increased borrowing abroad represents new issues by Canadian governments and their agencies. As the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) pointed out, the federal government, in effect, forces the provinces and corporations to enter the foreign market because it literally dries up any loose cash floating around in meeting its operating deficit.
We have to ask ourselves, what causes this need to borrow? Surely, it is not normal spending. Surely, if all governments had embarked upon normal spending practices we certainly would not have accumulated such a deficit. We, as Canadians, are among the highest taxed in the world, and yet our tax dollars are not enough. 1 suppose something could be said about the fact that Canadians are perhaps the most overgoverned people in the world. Because of that, governments have embarked upon poorly planned, extravagant and ineffective spending programs and money has been committed by governments without proper cost-benefit analyses and without having any idea as to the long-term implications with respect to cost or the efficacy of those particular programs.
In this country we have a growing penchant for direct government intervention. Every day we rely more and more upon the government to solve our problems, economic, social or otherwise, and in many respects this is a sad situation for Canadians because there is a tremendous amount of competence and expertise within the private sector and among individuals for dealing with day-to-day needs. For example, in the area of job creation much more could be done within the
Governmental Debt
private sector, given the proper incentives and proper tax policies, to encourage productivity and employment; but this government seems consistently to embark upon direct job creation programs by government means.
We have a situation where industry is over-regulated. We spend money on silly things like metric conversion and televising the proceedings of the House. These are items at which we could take a second look and could cut back our total commitment to the expenditure of funds. In that connection I want to place on the record an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen. It was written by a gentleman, Douglas Fullerton, who in the past has been notably sympathetic to the Liberal party. The article is entitled "Dear Pierre", and reads as follows:
Most of your new or expanded programs were concocted by a group of your colleagues, the "liberal" or spending wing, perhaps more appropriately designated as the "drunken sailors". With your support, their schemes were powered through cabinet and caucus, despite the doubts of more cautious ministers and members.
He goes on to say:
Of course, your open-handedness has not been all your fault-you have been egged on by some of the big-time spenders across the parliamentary floor, led by the NDP.
I think that, in a couple of short phrases, really summarizes the mentality of this administration. We do not see any end to this. For example, when we look at the new transportation act we find that here, again, we are going to see a tremendous shift in power to the hands of the Minister of Transport. This might be all right if there were any degree of stability on the government benches, but the game of musical chairs which is being played by the ministers and by the bureaucrats will create a great deal of uncertainty in the transportation field. If it is going to be operated by the whims of politicians and bureaucrats, I do not hold out a great deal of hope for providing good transportation service in this country, nor if there are going to be any more fiascos like the Pickering issue or the $46.5 million loss at Mirabel which we will have to pick up this year, nor if we are going to have the "user pay" concept as it applies for example in the case of the Calgary airport. These expensive concoctions will be billed to the users, namely, passengers on various airlines.
The government has not been a worthy partner in dealing with the problems of inflation and government spending. The problem we have is that when these programs are put into effect they generate bureaucracies. The bureaucracies become irreversible, they grow constantly, and new ways and new schemes for spending money are constantly being devised. As time goes by, in many cases the original purposes of these programs are totally forgotten. The money keeps pouring in. The tilt of our progressive system of taxation is such that the government always manages to pick up tax dollars as a result of increases in salaries and the progression of inflation. We all know how politically difficult it is to abandon programs. Information Canada and the CYC are just two recent examples. Programs are very difficult to withdraw, so I think it is imperative that this House be very reluctant to pass legislation at random and to develop programs readily on an ad hoc basis.

February 15, 1977
Governmental Debt
I think we should provide a more favourable climate for individuals in the private sector to deal with the day to day issues and problems thrust upon them throughout their lives. Governments are certainly needed, but they should not be the end-all in dealing with the problems we have to face.
It could be summed up in the words of the Auditor General in his last report to parliament-the kind of mentality there is within the bureaucracy-the mentality for creating a greater penetration by the government bureaucracy. At page 6 of the Conspectus the Auditor General said:
A senior official told me recently that, for many years, recognition and rewards have gone to those who devise ingenious new programs, rather than to those charged with the responsibility of restraining and controlling expenditures and ensuring that value is obtained for money spent.
What possible result could have occurred from such a practice other than the wild spending spree we have been on for the past ten years? That statement indicates to me that for public servants there are no rewards for efficiency or economy, but rather for empire building. We know also from the reports of the Auditor General that parliamentary control is being and has been circumvented in the never-ending squeeze for money. This has reached crisis level.
That brings me to the next statement of the Auditor General, who said:
I am deeply concerned that, on the evidence of the two-year examination carried out by the audit office, parliament and, indeed, the government, has lost or is close to losing effective control of the public purse.
This brings into focus parliament's inability to examine, to scrutinize, to challenge government spending in an effective way. I think that is the core of the problem. It is a damning indictment by a qualified man, backed by some 75 professional auditors across the country. The Auditor General pointed out that he chose his words very, very carefully when he made that statement. It is a very serious statement, and I think it is endorsed by R. S. Malone of the Globe and Mail who, on February 24, 1976, had this to say:
For ten years it has been abundantly clear where the government was taking our country. Our politicians during all these years, unfortunately, were more occupied in trying to buy popularity with over-spending-and manufacturing money to pay for it all...
In a ten year period, Ottawa increased its spending by 600 per cent. It could only be paid for with devalued dollars, or legal counterfeiting, and Ottawa has known this all the time.
In summary, that means we are simply financing today's luxuries against the labours of tomorrow.
For the past two or three months there has been a great deal of interest in Crown corporations and their management. These corporations are recipients of vast sums of public money. For example, a question placed on the order paper on October 20 by the hon. member for York-Simcoe shows that in terms of government of Canada advances, loans and investments in Crown corporations, the total is $21 billion. That is taxpayers' money. The problem with Crown corporations is insufficient accountability. In many cases there is essentially no accountability to parliament and the shareholders, that is,

the people of Canada. On that subject the Auditor General has this to say:
In the majority of the Crown corporations, audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control is weak and ineffective. Moreover, co-ordination and guidance by central government agencies of financial management and control practices in these Crown corporations are virtually non-existent.
He went on to say that whatever mechanisms were in place were grossly inadequate. While this is a very, very serious statement, what causes one to chuckle is the fact that the government is unable to provide a committee of this House with a list of the Crown corporations. It sounds unbelievable, but it is true. In testimony before the Public Accounts Committee on February 10, 1977, at pages 14:10 and 14:11, Mr. D. L. Meyers of the Auditor General's office revealed that no one in the government had a list of all Crown corporations. The Auditor General's officer prepared one and found over 30 not listed and apparently not subject to the rules of financial management provided by the Financial Administration Act. That is incredible, yet we have a continuing proliferation of Crown corporations and appendages in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF FEDERAL, PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL DEBT
speechtext: Are you surprised?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF FEDERAL, PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL DEBT
speechtext:
No, I am not surprised, but I am shocked and angry. When we have witnessed the revelations regarding AECF and Polysar we can understand how such problems occur and why we do not even know how many Crown corporations we have. Surely we have to question the competence of the directors and management of Polysar and AECL. Surely the responsibilities charged to them have largely been ignored. Enormous payments have been made to unknown people. There has been circumvention of foreign laws, and the government has simply failed to act or has acquiesced.
It is clear that the government has used Crown corporations as a vehicle for government departments to evade and circumvent parliamentary control. They become nothing more than reward centres for the heelers and bagmen. They have become tantamount to the Senate.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but my time is running short. I will conclude by saying the government is now syphoning off 41 per cent or 42 per cent of the gross national product. The federal share has grown rapidly, while municipal governments have been squeezed by both senior levels of government. Federal spending rose by 14 per cent this year, and will rise by 11 per cent or 12 per cent next year. The year before that it was some 18 per cent. I do not find this consistent with the empty promise of keeping government's expenditure in line with the growth in gross national product. Talk of cutbacks and restraint is comical when we know that we will see three or four sets of supplementary estimates.
We must ask if there is a solution and if we will ever be able to deal with the issue referred to in this motion. It seems to me we have to consider seriously the growth, power and size of the bureaucracy. We have to address ourselves to this problem of mismanagement in Crown corporations in which is involved a large amount of taxpayers' dollars. We have to consider
February 15, 1977

seriously a better vehicle for planning and evaluating our programs, and the impact of further centralization. Above all, we must ensure that parliamentary authority is restored.
To achieve some of these goals the first thing we must do is honour the recommendation of the Auditor General and appoint a Comptroller General. On this the Auditor General had the following to say:
... will lay the essential foundation of a soundly conceived program for restoring effective control over public funds and assets, and for ensuring probity, prudence and economy in their management.
Second, the increasing trend toward centralization of government must stop. Local governments can, if permitted breathing room, do an effective and efficient job of providing service to Canadians. In a country as vast and diverse as Canada, local governments can provide a much broader form of government service.
Third, and in conclusion, it is important for the government to consider seriously the establishment of an effective program review agency, an agency which would be responsible for the independent evaluation of all programs involving government spending. I suggest that such programs ought to be examined by an independent-I stress independent-source early in their lives, probably in the second year of operation. Established programs should be subject to ongoing evaluations as to efficacy and cost. I suggest thorough cost-benefit analyses should be performed, to ensure that the Canadian public is getting its money's worth for every dollar spent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF FEDERAL, PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL DEBT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I should like to thank the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) for introducing the motion under consideration which is of the utmost importance when one considers Canada's financial situation at this time.
On many occasions, the Creditistes presented the same subject for discussion in the House because it is not only of vital importance to them but also to the economy in general, in particular when one considers the financial situation of various public agencies and I cannot mention many of them today because time is running out.
At the moment I have in mind the financial problems faced by some municipalities in my riding and in some neighbouring towns. Last week, in my riding the whole city council resigned because of a serious financial situation. The problem is now left with the provincial government. More than 46 per cent of this municipality's budget goes to pay the interest on the municipal debt.
More than 58 per cent of the budget of St. Hubert, a town near Montreal, goes to pay the interest on the public debt. 1 could carry on, Mr. Speaker and give you a list of nearly all the municipal governments in Quebec in a difficult financial position.
Before going any further, I would like to say a few words about the new Quebec government as it faces the municipal
Governmental Debt
problem. One does not know yet the solution they will propose, but at least they said the day following the elections or a few days later that they would grant municipalities and towns discretionary subsidies. The government used to decide which towns were to receive a subsidy, which should not, thereby creating discrimination among various municipal governments which led to a situation where these last ten years, some municipal governments were in highly abnormal position compared to others. For instance municipalities with 15,000 people would receive $100,000 from the provincial government whereas others with 50,000 or 60,000 people did not receive anything due to the discretionary policy of the Liberal government in Quebec. Therefore, I am looking forward to see at the provincial and at the federal levels, taxation and monetary policies whereby municipal governments, towns and school boards would know where they are going and which sort of support they can count on for the next two, five or ten years. Under the present system, all the municipal governments in Quebec are completely in the dark which explains why many of our councillors are now hitting the roof in front of the financial situation which confronts them.
Mr. Speaker, the motion under consideration today proposes a monetary reform. We are asking the government to issue new funds through the Bank of Canada and to stop private interests and intermediaries, namely banking institutions from creating public funds.

Finance public enterprise with public funds (that is, with new money created by the government, through the Bank of Canada, and issued as interest-free loans for such projects); Finance private enterprise with private funds (that is, with the savings of the people).
... we now have a dual-economy, consisting of both public enterprise, and .. . the two should be Financed on different bases .. .
The government's incredibly stupid and utterly needless practice of borrowing Canadian money, at interest, means that the taxpayers are saddled with the burden of paying about $5 billion in interest, each year, for which they receive virtually nothing whatever in return. This payment of huge amounts of unearned interest, which represents no corresponding new production, is a major cause of the present inflation and is largely responsible for our excessive taxes.
The government's practice of Financing public projects with private funds (that is, with money borrowed, at interest, from private moneylenders) is doubly inflationary. Not only does it cause an excessive increase in the amount of money in circulation but, at the same time, it also tends to very greatly decrease production. When the people are urged to buy interest-bearing government bonds, the government is saying to them, in effect: 0Why bother to invest your money in private productive enterprise? Lend it to us instead and we will guarantee you a high rate of interest on it, with no work and no risk whatever on your part. The real producers will be taxed to pay you this unearned interest.' How much longer shall the private moneylenders be allowed to thus sabotage our system of encouraging and rewarding initiative in private enterprise?
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, billions of dollars are now being invested in the public sector. Those billions of dollars come from the savings of Canadians and are created with a stroke of a pen by the savings bonds of the federal, provincial and municipal governments as well as school boards. The billions of dollars invested in building roads, bridges, schools and hospitals are unproductive. The financing formula we advocate for the public sector will have the effect of releasing those billions of unproductive dollars so they may be invested in the private

February 15, 1977
Governmental Debt
sector. We believe that profit is a legitimate goal and that savings invested in businesses are entitled to a return and would find there a terrific opportunity of serving the common good by helping the country progress.
The savings released from the public sector could be invested in residential construction which would provide an opportunity for profitable investments and serve highly social purposes. The savings diverted from the public to the private sector would also provide businesses with an abundant source of capital. Canadian businesses would less and less have to turn to foreign investors and foreign banks to sell bonds and shares to provide for their financing. This way, Canadians could finance the economic development of their own country.
Mr. Speaker, it is rather easy to understand that private profit-making businesses must pay interest-and that is normal. On the other hand, public businesses such as the federal and provincial governments, municipalities and school boards which are non profit-making organizations designed to provide the community with services should have to pay interest. That is why we in the Social Credit Party of Canada advocate an economy where public capital would be financed with public capital and private enterprise should be financed with private capital. The savers, those who convert their money, their savings in savings bonds could convert them in company shares that could be guaranteed by the government of Canada and the provinces to prevent private businesses from being faced with the problem of financing their businesses.
Mr. Speaker, I do not have enough time to quote all relevant figures, but those interests stand out as the cause of those huge umpayable debts and taxes stiffling all sectors of our economy. I do not intend to refer to the figures of economists quoted this afternoon by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), some economists who are paid to advocate the present system. I would like to refer, Mr. Speaker, to the Reader's Digest of Januray, 1977 which also has economists and takes a more realistic view of things. I quote:

Quiz on Taxes and Government Spending Total taxes paid by the average Canadian family, including direct and indirect taxation imposed by all levels of government, increased by 85 per cent between 1969 and 1975 because government spending at all levels has soared.

Mr. Speaker, between 1969 and 1975 taxes increased by 85 per cent, more than 14 per cent a year; this means that in seven years taxes will have gone up 100 per cent in Canada. [English]
Moreover, governments spend much more than they take from us in taxes.
[ Translation]
The government is spending more money than it is getting through taxation.

In this way they have contributed to the inflation that depletes the value of every dollar we earn ...

The national debt-the amount Ottawa must borrow to make up what it has spent beyond income, is soaring past $25 billion.
[ Translation]
I am still quoting from the Januray 1977 issue of the Reader's Digest:

In ten years, the budget has skyrocketed 350 per cent from $8.8 billion to a forecast $39 billion in this fiscal year (April 1, 1976 to March 31, 1977).
Total government spending per person was $2,900 in 1975. But the governments took in only $2,700 per person. Thus they have proceeded to spend an additional inflationary $200 on each of us! And government spending has increased over 100 per cent per person since 1970 . ..
The national debt of the federal government will be around $28 billion at the end of the fiscal year, the result of budget deficits in 20 out of the last 23 years.

Mr. Speaker, I want to draw your attention to the fact that during the last 23 years we had 20 budget deficits yet neither the Progressive Conservatives nor the Liberals have changed their policy on this point for both have produced budget deficits.

All these answers are correct.

speechtext:
I think the hon. member's point will be well taken. It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock this evening.
At six o'clock the House took recess.



*

February 15, 1977
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock, I was reading from an article published in the Reader's Digest of January 1, 1977 dealing with Canada's financial situation and related to the motion moved today by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert). I was referring to paragraph 5 of this article. [English]
The interest on the national debt, which was already $1.2 billion in 1967 will be around $4.6 billion at the end of this fiscal year, making it the third largest federal expenditure after health and welfare and economic development and support. Last year, the government guaranteed $15.5 billion in loans and advances to Crown corporations, of which about $7 billion went to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The government also guarantees loans made by charter banks to certain groups, including the wheat board, farmers, fishermen and students.
Federal spending has grown faster in the past ten years than the private economy which supports it. While GNP tripled, federal spending increased from $10 billion in 1967 to roughly $41 billion this Fiscal year. Some $12.4 billion was spent on social welfare programs during the last Fiscal year. Defence expenditures, however, amounted to only $2.6 billion while government outlays on activities associated with Canada's natural resources and primary industry amounted to $3.2 billion. Under the government's bilingualism program, expenditures reached $121 million.
From each dollar of national income, federal, provincial and municipal tax collectors take 42 cents of which 22 cents goes to Ottawa. Tax revenues have been rising consistently since the mid-1950's. If public spending continues on its present course it will not be long before the government takes more than 50 cents from each dollar in taxes.
Government at all levels employs 1.8 million people, teachers and armed forces included. That is one out of every five in the labour force. It is the largest employer in the country, spending over $10 billion on salaries and wages. Federal employees, excluding the armed forces, were paid about $5 billion in 1975, roughly triple the $1.7 billion they were earning in 1965. Between 1965 and 1975, the consumer price index rose 72 per cent. At that rate, a dollar saved today will be worth only six cents 50 years from now.

Mr. Speaker, this is a shocking figure considering that the increase in the cost of living in the last 10 years was 72 percent. Taking into account, as the Minister of Supply and services (Mr. Goyer) said this afternoon, the fact that our national product amounts to approximately $175 billion and then what the Reader's Digest has to say, it means that inflation apart, our $175 billion gross national product for 1976 will come up to about $55 billion in constant dollars of 1965.
It means that our national production in constant or current dollars has hardly increased during the last ten years. We could say that the national production amounts to about $175 billion, but if we consider the cost of living we can say that the production did not progress during the last decade. However, in 1867, when our Confederation came into being, the national debt in Canada was $93,046,051; in 1900, our debt reached $346 million and fifty years after Confederation, our debt hit $3 billion, totalling ten years later, in 1943, $9,228 billion; in 1955, it was at $17,952 million and in 1967, public expenses, of all government levels amounted to $21.8 million to rise up
Governmental Debt
to $55 million in 1974, an average increase of 14 per cent a year; that constitutes 32.9 per cent of our gross national product in 1967 and 39.1 per cent in 1974.
Mr. Speaker, that tremendous increase certainly indicates the continuing trend of governments appropriating a larger part of economic profits in this country.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, hardly 100 years after Confederation, the federal debt in Canada had soared by almost 60,000 per cent. I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian population increased sixfold since Confederation, but over the same time the public debt went up by almost 600 fold. So every day Canadians have to shell out almost $10 million in taxes merely to pay interest on the national debt.
How many bridges, hospitals, public schools, utilities will not be built for Canadians because of that $10 million a day? Ten million a day to help investors getting richer while Canadian taxpayers are waiting for services which they are entitled to and for which they paid taxes. We all know, Mr. Speaker, that the governments which let the public debt spiral out of control are responsible for that shameful waste, that is $10 million a day spent public debt service. That money should be used to meet the needs of Canadians, not to enrich financiers.
Mr. Speaker, several years ago, more specifically in May 1934, before the Bank of Canada was established under Bill C-19, when the Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce was discussing the possible establishment of such a bank, there was in the British Columbia legislature a Liberal member who was to become a member of this House in 1935, and later a senator. Referring back to pages 500 to 800 of that committee's proceedings, we find that the Liberal member's suggestions to the committee are still extremely significant and relevant in 1976-77. I am referring to the Hon. G. G. McGeer, a Vancouver lawyer, MLA for Vancouver Burrard, who appeared on May 1, 1934. I would like to quote him from page 503, since his evidence is quite relevant to the motion now before us:
Under our system, there is no reason why mercantile banks should not keep doing what they have been doing until now, that is serving private interests. But when it comes to allowing a private banker to lay his hands on public credit and manage it to his own benefit as a monopoly, it is time all public leaders got involved, because under the present system, we are leasing the nation's public credit to a group of Financiers who manage it with two goals in mind, first to serve the monopoly's private interests, and then to maintain the consumers' purchasing power and support the taxpayers' ability to pay. But unfortunately the latter aim has been sorely neglected. So much so in fact that across the Dominion ...
. . . that was during the depression . . .
... municipal, provincial and national bankruptcy is widespread, the social system is in complete chaos.
I could go on quoting page after page of this extremely interesting evidence. On page 54 of the book Let's Talk Money and Banking, Arthur I. Judge, editor of the Baltimore Canning Trade, said the following:
For over a century, the management of the monetary system has been entrusted to bankers and finance specialists, in blind faith and absolute confidence.

February 15, 1977
Governmental Debt
Necessity now forces us to do away with bankers' management, and let governments manage public funds and control and direct the monetary system.
By giving these privileges back to the government, democracy will take over from the oligarchic power that bankers now have on government and trade.
Thanks to these changes, the elected representatives of the people will become the masters of the "economic arteries" of the nation, and it will be possible to maintain a responsible government on democratic principles.
No one has the right to say that the establishment of such a democracy cannot and will not lead to progress and prosperity as long as governments are not given a chance as were bankers, to control the monetary system.
The government should now take power away from bankers or the mismanaging of public funds will destroy the government and bring the civilization that generated it to an end.
The right hon. Prime Minister said is this House that provincial governments had only to ask for financial reforms, but I must remind him that, on the 20th of March 1934, as can be read in the minutes, under the title Money, Credit and Unemployment, the British Columbia parliament adopted the following resolution:
Whereas the monetary value of the exchange of goods and services inside the Dominion of Canada has fallen from more than $46,000,000,000 in 1929 to less than $30,000,000,000 in 1933; and
Whereas this decline in domestic trade has been followed by a disastrous increase in unemployment in Canada;
Whereas, pursuant to the constitution, the Parliament of the Dominion of Canada has exclusive jurisdiction over the creation, issuance and circulation of purchasing power in the form of money and credit belonging to the people of this province-
It is therefore resolved that in the opinion of this Assembly, the state should set up a national banking system to distribute national, provincial and municipal credit to keep in circulation a sufficient amount of purchasing power in dollars and cents and that the national, provincial and municipal credit should be used to alleviate the present burden of taxation and unemployment as well as to help restore and maintain Canada's prosperity.
It is also resolved that this Assembly declare itself in favour of a determined plan ...
And not decided upon blindly, in an ad hoc context, on a day-to-day basis ...
... of effective co-operation between national, provincial, municipal authorities ...
That is what we are asking for.
... and the proposed banking system, to use public credit, monetized in the form of purchasing power, to implement an important program of public works designed to help the country and provide an income to its people, and to use as well the public credit thus monetized for expenditures required for the good administration of this country, its provinces and municipalities, school boards as well as social services which are vital to maintain education, health, peace, satisfaction, and freedom of all citizens of Canada with a minimum of expenses to taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, before the Bank of Canada Act was passed in 1935, G. G. McGeer, a Liberal member, had warned this House and said: "Let us not make the same mistake as ancient Rome which brought about its ruin by entrusting bankers and financiers with public credit, and let us not provoke at home the same disasters which happened in Rome by surrendering national revenues to the public sector and allowing the latter to make overly big profits in taxes levied in the wealth of other vicious systems."
Mr. Speaker, it means that when the government collects high taxes today, it is to pay back mainly interests on the public debt. As I am running out of time, Mr. Speaker, I

would like to refer to what G. G. McGeer said in 1934, and it is still relevant in 1977 since at present we have entrusted private institutions, which are called banks, with the administration or control of our currency, our credit, which represents 94 per cent of the money supply in Canada.
The Creditistes want the banks to carry on their financial transactions but not to manufacture money. The Bank of Canada which was established in 1935 has only been a "cover-up" for the chartered banks which today operate within the Bank of Canada because the federal government does not discharge its responsibilities and does not manage the finances of the country on its own. The federal government by issuing federal bonds, gives the banks the power to monetize the credit of the nation to let the country in debt and to make us pay now 50c for each dollar that is paid in taxes to the government of Canada, for the repayment of the interest on our provincial, municipal, federal and school board debts.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to discuss in the House today in the presence of all our colleagues, a subject as important as this, namely the Bank of Canada. We, French-Canadians have a reputation to speak often about culture and language but rather seldom on financial matters. And yet owing to some of our French-Canadians colleagues opposite, we have the opportunity to-day to consider an important subject and I am convinced that this congenial and friendly discussion will make our colleagues, the other members of the House of Commons, realize that we are all concerned about financial problems.
Above partisanship, Mr. Speaker, it remains however that the basic matters of concern in our modern society are financial matters and even though the concern we share is the same in principle it does not always meet in certain areas because we often deal with it in different ways. And from this confrontation of ideas and solutions we have a richer society. If I consider the preamble or what is in fact the substance of the motion of today I read the following and I quote:
This House notes with distress the prodigious increase in the federal, provincial and municipal debt, which will result in the shattering of our country . ..
However incredible as it may seem, I share most of the concern of my colleagues opposite. I can see that our citizens are concerned with an increase in the debt of governments rather than with individual solutions to solve these problems.
Mr. Speaker, I think I voice the concern of all my colleagues when I support government commitments at all levels, federal, provincial and municipal, in respect of the social duty we must perform towards all individuals, and particularly toward the underprivileged. But I am not the only one who finds that the first concern of those known as our leaders is not to assume their responsibilities but to pass them on to the government level, and no doubt I am not the only one who deplores that the self-styled leaders of society at every level have become afraid of responsibilities, those who believe that governments are there to meet every demand submitted to them.
February 15, 1977

Mr. Speaker, I think that the Canadian society has tremendous advantages that I do not intend to appraise or stress, but I find that even the present society experiences exceptional difficulties, because its members are inclined not to assume the responsibilities that are theirs. If governments at all levels are so excessively in debt, that comes from the weakness of governments because they say yes to all requests put before them. That is because of the poor sense of responsibility of our leaders at all levels who, with a view to getting their responsibilities off their hands, apply to governments as if they were wonder governments, able to give at any time, under any circumstances, a favourable answer to everyone asking for money.
Mr. Speaker, as a French-speaking Canadian, as a full member of this House, I am glad to be able to demonstrate tonight with my colleagues opposite that the problems our government is facing will be resolved under the condition that our colleagues opposite collaborate with us to find solutions. When I ask this to my colleagues opposite, I know that they are aware that our governments need some participation, some collaboration from every member without any party considerations, because what is important is not to win acceptance for one's own political idea, but first of all to win acceptance for this idea of one Canada of which the flag is a concrete example, the flag beside our distinguished Speaker who does his utmost to give to every member of this House the rights to which they are entitled.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is becoming important to realize that the problems we face are not unsolvable. Sometimes we tend to exaggerate situations and it is sometimes normal, in all fields, in order to give a faithful image of a situation, to caricature it.
That's the same as the Creditistes?

No, it is not the same! What I mean is that in our society, there is a tendency to picture problems as though they were tragic. I suggest it is a better way to explain, and above all to say things. Mr. Speaker, tonight I am particularly happy to take part in this debate, not in the hope of bringing revolutionary solutions, original solutions that will solve all our problems, but I feel that what inspires all those who bring their contribution to this debate, their first concern, is to help Canadians, and particularly those who are least privileged.
We, who are here, cannot say we are underprivileged. I think we all enjoy a fairly high standard of living, that we all enjoy socio-economic advantages that are admittedly above average. But I do think it is our concern, our duty, our responsibility to help those who are less fortunate. And when I hear my colleagues across the way express their concern by suggesting solutions that may not be new, but have some value, in an effort to solve the problems, I feel that we cannot shrug off people who, like us, are trying to find solutions.
This evening, as I read the motion before the House, I see it is expressed in extremely restrained terms. When, for instance, one reads this, and I quote:
Governmental Debt
That this House further regrets the fact that the government has failed to advance any new formula for financing the public sector to correct this situation...
I am almost willing to conclude that the warning sounded by our colleagues is of value because, considering the problems facing us, we have to conclude that we have failed to find a real solution. Let us be honest about the situation. We should not dismiss any solution offering some possibility of helping those who are less well-off than we are. To my mind, the debate until now has maintained a desirable level, which allows us to conclude that we are not here to try to destroy by the use of words that exceed our thoughts, words that win acceptance for political ideas or that pave the way for an eventual election.
We are given here the opportunity to note together, in a fraternal and friendly atmosphere, that Canada, an extremely rich country is nevertheless beset with problems which we have not been able to solve. I trust some of my suggestions will be followed, and that studies will be encouraged in that sense, that an attempt will be made to understand what ails that infamous monetary system, why we are controlled by a group of people who deprive everyone; even though Canada is rich, as I said at the beginning, tremendously rich, it is inhabited by people a high percentage of whom are poor in the midst of that wealth.

Mr. Speaker, first, let me tell you how pleased I am to take part in this debate because as concerns the indebtedness of governments, public bodies and municipalities, I share the same concern as my colleagues of the Social Credit party, although I would not propose the same solutions which I find simplistic. I may perhaps echo an old story that we have been hearing back home for 12 years and that I am still hearing in the House after more than two years.
I wish to point out the difference between an opposition member who can always ask for more regardless of cost and a government member who must decide on priorities and appropriate and redistribute public funds. I blame my Creditistes colleagues for exploiting the people's credibility by harping on the same string, but to be more positive, I would rather urge them to go deeper in search of solutions. I feel that for my colleagues opposite, it is a marketing problem, and they should understand that the House of Commons is the place where it is most difficult to understand, first because most people do not buy anything for want of money and second because those who would normally buy have quite different demands, as their mandate is quite different. However, I agree that we stop to think and try to find means to rectify a situation which could become catastrophic when I consider that the federal government had a deficit of some $4 billion last year, that the province of Quebec alone had a deficit of more than $1 billion and that my own little town with a population of 7,000 and with a budget of $1.7 billion might have an annual deficit of nearly $100,000 as things are. But if this discussion is just an oral dispute, there will be two causes for the catastrophe instead of one. I think we can come back to the proposal of our colleague, the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne), who told us we should look at our own budgets; there is certainly a way to face debts very efficiently, namely by deciding not to run into debt. This gives us the advantage of not having to pay interests which we find extravagant.

February 15, 1977

Therefore we should make sure that our constituents are committed to such a philosophy because there lies the only possible solution. Everything depends on the ability to pay of the Canadian taxpayers and on their free choice, insofar as they can make a choice. Therefore, it becomes a matter of conscience and knowledge, a matter of priority and personal choice. Thus what we must protect is the ability of the citizen to make a choice through adequate information, a participatory system and, finally, through real participation to the decision making process. The government should respect his mandate and, the opposition should perhaps see to it that the government is doing so, instead of putting words in other people's mouth to please a few.
I should like to say, however, that the matter raised by the Social Credit has merit and that together we should try to find possible solution. Indeed, it is useful and even absolutely necessary that thogether we should consider the financial position of our country; I would even go as far as to that what the opposition did today might be useful, provided that the proposed solution is understandable and intelligent, and the motion, in its present form, puzzles me. One thing is sure the phenomenal increase of the debt-be it federal, provincial, municipal, of the school boards and even of many taxpayers- must stop because the day of reckoning will come soon and the money will have to be available.
I think that, even in the most honorable and generous schemes, it is a problem which has to be solved right from the start and the government should see to it that these restrictions and reasonable request are accepted by the great majority of the people.
There is no magic formula. If goods and services are purchased, they will have to be paid. And if our liberalism can be faulted, it is for going too far, for getting people into the habit of requesting and receiving ever more. As a rule, they were always asking for more and good governments were those which were giving more. At present, a good government is the most reasonable, the one which will make people think. Why? Because otherwise they will all become slaves to their wishes, because our resources will exceed our ability to pay. And this is how rich people grow ever richer, and the poor who do not know how to ask but are only able to wait are becoming poorer in comparison with the rich.
I believe all Canadians can make that effort to think and understand because to protect oneself is also to protect others. Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal for a few moments with taxation at the municipal level. Surely we all agree that this is a real disaster, but I want to point out that the debt at the municipal level is neither a prerogative nor an initiative of the federal government. The fact is, however, that the taxation problem at the municipal level is such that we must absolutely find a solution and I think this initiative should come first from the provincial jurisdiction, and this is more than just devising a balanced budget formula.
The basic problem at the municipal level, and I speak from experience as a mayor, is that municipal governments are too
[Mr. Tcssicr.j
dependant upon funds on which they have no control. I will quote as an example my own municipal budget which I had to administer and which amounts to some $1,700,000. In this budget, taxes amount to $726,000, compensation accounts for more than $56,000. exchanges of services for $280,000, local revenues total $400,000 but there are also revenues from outside, such as the sales tax which represents $494,000 and grants for $106,000. Therefore you will note that out of a budget of $1.7 million, $601,000 came from outside the municipality and in most cases, these are revenues which vary from year to year, and therefore which we cannot take for granted.
What is wrong is that people get used to receiving and finally they get the impression that everything is due to them. But we also create a state of dependence which changes from year to year. In addition there is the matter of bookkeeping; people cannot unravel figures from year to year and then they start having doubts about their administration.
To conclude, in municipal taxation there is only one accountant for the municipality, but as everybody is a rate payer the people should know why they pay and require that the money be used for the purposes for which they pay. It's a matter of discharging our responsibilities. There will be room for changes from time to time, always according to the wishes of the population-and the regulations of various systems and their size can change the regulations themselves.
At the present time, when we talk about Quebec and Canada, we should be careful not to confuse the issues. There is the government of Quebec, which assumes power in time and space. There are also the intentions of the P.Q., I mean the Parti Quebecois, to separate Quebec, which is not included in what we consider the mandate of the Levesque government, namely the good management of Quebec affairs.
In my opinion, my colleague from Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) has perfectly managed to confuse all the issues. His party should clearly explain its position. Do they want the separation of Quebec, do they want to join that movement? If so, let there be no confusion. If not, they should be responsible and honest enough to say yes to Canada. We should pay tribute to men like Robert Stanfield and Real Caouette who were also members of the opposition but who have always put Canada's unity above petty, partisan considerations and if the week-end reports had any basis I think that the present leader should heed this warning. Besides, Mr. Speaker, I would have liked more details from the opposition, and particularly from the Social Credit party of Canada, as far as the open attack against the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is concerned. To my mind, DREE, though, at the beginning, it was created to solve regional disparities, is the only instrument we now have, especially in rural areas, to help industries.
This is the question I ask: do we want to help industries in rural areas? Yes or no? Of course, I can see that the risks are greater in our areas because business people are obviously fewer, I think that they have as much merit, if not more, as the
February 15, 1977

experienced industrialists of the great urban areas. Should we keep on trusting the small businessman trying to assess the risks, but should we continue to help the industries in our rural areas? To say that it is merely Liberal patronage is another gratuitous statement, and if there is to be some discussion, it will be about the application of the principle of assistance to industry, wherever it may be in Canada. Questions may be asked, but if charges are laid, they should be substantiated.
Secondly, in the specific area of health and welfare, particularly the guaranteed income for the handicapped-and I wish it would come as soon as possible-are we prepared to say yes or no? But the ever recurring question is: where will the money come from? More taxes, fewer services, other priorities. I also heard my colleagues across the way talk about increased pensions, pensions at 60, pensions at 50, pensions to spouses, and so on. Such aims are most commendable, but one thing is certain: where will that money come from? We agree on finding it together, but please, do not delude yourselves into thinking that services will be maintained without the required money, if not through further taxes or readjustments within the existing systems.
Third, with respect to housing there is talk, for example, of low cost rental units, particularly for elderly people or for the handicapped. Very complicated calculations are made to show how much buildings will cost. We are told that this building will pay for itself twice, three times, four and a half times. I think the real question to be asked is: are the Canadian people now prepared to provide that service for older people or the handicapped? If they are prepared to pay for such a service, then it might be possible and desirable to have the necessary calculations made in order to determine what such projects actually cost. For my part, I consider that people are now in favour of projects such as low cost rental units, homes for older people, even hospitals, schools. We are talking about a choice; this is a mandate we have to carry out and we intend to stand by it.
Fourth, I should also like to deal with agriculture, and particularly the milk policy that was severely criticized by the opposition and the press during the past year. It is a fact that in 1975-76, while the operating budget for the policy had been set at approximately $275 million, the cost to the government was in the order of $535 million. The government had no choice, it was a necessity, but some $535 million still had to be found.
In 1976-77, normally, the budget should have been in the order of $290 million, but we knew that we had to pay surpluses. The budget had been set at $631 million and during the year the government agreed to add an additional $10 million which brought the budget to a record $641 million in support of the milk industry as well as farming and rural economies.

Does this really mean that the government will agree to find the required sums? Where, and instead of what priority?
In reality, it is always the same question. It is possible to have a multitude of projects. I believe that if after honest and sincere reflection we can come to a general consensus in the House, as my colleague said earlier, I believe it is possible to find solutions if we can forget party politics, and particularly partisan politics.
School boards have also been mentioned. I think we must be honest enough to admit once again that the federal government as such has no responsibility in this area, but we must also note that to reduce the powers of the school boards, a relationship dependency has been created towards the provincial government and the cost of this dependency has been excessive centralization and a nearly complete loss of power on the part of school boards themselves. I feel that we, on this side of the House, must not delve upon this whole matter of the Bank of Canada but, like the others, we must take the time to consider the control of public finances and we are ready to do so, by reasonable and acceptable means. In conclusion, I would add that it is important to curb expenses and severely restrict the services we have become accustomed to in order to reshuffle priorities. Otherwise we will have to pay and since the paying capacity of the government, public agencies and individuals is limited, we will necessarily have to learn or relearn how to live within our means.

Mr. Speaker, in the five minutes or so that are left, I would like, with your permission, to draw a very short conclusion from today's debate, free of all political partisanship. Having heard the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Tessier) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) it seems to me that our message got through.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to thank very briefly my colleague, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) and commend him for bringing forth this motion. My colleague, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) has touched upon the constitutional aspect of the financial problems of our country. My colleague, the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) dealt with the role of public and private assets with regards to the dealings of the House committees, to show that the idea we are touching upon today follows modern problems that have been around for a long time and my colleague, the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) has defined the role of public and private assets in our country in a very efficient and vivid way.
In this respect we have heard the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) claim that provinces had enough with one-fifth per cent of federal general revenues. We have heard the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) say that time has come to sit down, leave aside any partisan spirit and consider the increase in the debt of our public bodies at federal, provincial or municipal levels, as it is a major problem. We have just heard our colleague from Compton (Mr. Tessier) raise the same question: Where are we going to find the money?
Mr. Speaker, the Social Crediters did not ask for any project. Today our party considered in a very positive way a problem which confronts every Canadian municipality in every

province of Canada, this Canada in which we believe indeed but, in answer to the hon. member for Compton, not at any cost. Today we moved a motion proposing that the Bank of Canada be used to intervene, not in the private sector but in the public sector so as to put an end to this endless process by which we are constantly running deeper into debt.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding my remarks I would like to give an example which seems fundamental to me. The House of Commons has two problems to solve as soon as possible. First the financing of our public sector at municipal, provincial and federal levels. One has only to recall the successive failures of the federal-provincial conferences of finance ministers and of the first ministers to see how urgent it is to find a solution to this question. The second priority for the House to deal with is the question of the unity of our country, the Canadian unity. For our party these are two related questions and they are deeply linked together. We cannot pretend to rewrite our constitution while preserving a system for Financing the public sector which was conceived a hundred years ago.
Mr. Speaker, this is a priority, so we repeat the proposal we made today that the government positively consider using the Bank of Canada to help provinces and municipalities.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GARRISON DIVERSION-PROPOSED TRUST FUND TO PAY FOR ALTERATIONS-ALTERNATE SOURCE OF WATER FOR PORTAGE LA PRAIRIE
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GARRISON DIVERSION-PROPOSED TRUST FUND TO PAY FOR ALTERATIONS-ALTERNATE SOURCE OF WATER FOR PORTAGE LA PRAIRIE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is leaving for the United States next week to meet with President Carter, I wish to make one final plea that he include the Garrison diversion project on his agenda and again request of the President that the United States stop work on parts of the Garrison project, namely, the Lonetree Reservoir and Velva Canal, the two sections of the project that will affect Canada and pollute Canadian waters.
This matter has been raised in the House dozens and dozens of times. The misleading answers we have received from the Prime Minister have been most disturbing, as is the lack of positive action by the government to request assurances from the United States government that Manitoba is protected. Last week the Prime Minister was asked if he would include the Garrison diversion project on his agenda. He gave a most
February 15, 1977

curious answer, stating in part, as reported at page 2775 of Hansard for February 7, 1977, that:
The hon. member is aware that that report has come out now and is before the IJC and is favourable to Canada.
It is not at all favourable to Canada. It calls for $50 million worth of projects to be changed in the diversion unit. 1 do not know how that can be considered as favourable to Canada. The Prime Minister went on to say:
We are expecting that the IJC will accept the conclusion of the report.
I do not know what the Prime Minister means when he says the IJC will accept the conclusion of the report. The IJC simply makes a report and presents it to both countries. It holds hearings. The IJC has no authority to force either country to take action. Instead of receiving answers from the Prime Minister to indicate that he will discuss the matter with the president and make certain that Manitoba is protected, we receive evasive, misleading answers.
Last week I asked the Prime Minister if, since the United States is ignoring the $1.2 million IJC study and continuing with two aspects of the project which will affect Manitoba waters, the Prime Minister would negotiate with the president to place $50 million in a trust fund, to allow for the alterations needed to the project. I also asked that a timetable be established for the work necessary on projects such as the $6 million alternate water supply which will be needed for the city of Portage la Prairie.
The northern Manitoba Commercial Fisherman's Association has also made representations to President Carter. In a letter sent to the president last week they stated that by 1980 the effects of the appearance of alien fish species into Manitoba water systems from the Missouri River watershed could result in a net loss of $5.2 million a year to Manitoba's commercial Fishermen.
You can see that this is a matter for concern, Mr. Speaker, why we are asking for straightforward answers and why we ask the Prime Minister to raise this question with President Carter next week.
Another matter of concern has to do with the fact that the government of Canada, in a note it sent to the United States in October, 1976, requested a specific moratorium on Lonetree. This request has not been answered by the State Department.
I point out that Congressman Dante Facell, chairman of the Subcommittee on International Political and Military Affairs and a member of the Committee on International Relations was concerned about the fact that the request by Canada has not been answered by the Department of State. All of this leads us to believe that present construction work is a breach of the promises and of faith between the two countries.
Lastly, I point out that the North Dakota legislature has been asking Congress to accelerate funding which would further that breach. It is a matter of concern that anyone should be asking for further funding of this project when the IJC
Adjournment Debate
report stated that modifications should be made to that project.
I am asking the Prime Minister to request the president to establish a trust fund which will allow for the $50 million to be spent on alterations which would cover such items as the McClusky canal fish screen modifications, which would cost $2 million; the installation of works to remove wasteways, which would cost $22 million; the Lonetree outlet works and filtration outlet, which would cost $1.9 million; the sand filtration involving the Velva Canal, which would cost $9 million; additional costs for membrane lining for the Velva Canada Canal, which would cost $14 million. In addition, there will be a need for an alternate water supply for the city of Souris; that will cost $1.5 million. As I said earlier, it wil) cost $6 million to establish an alternate water supply for the city of Portage la Prairie. As well, additional cost will be incurred every year for operating this water plant.
Work is being done on the Garrison diversion project, but we have no timetable and no idea when it will affect Canadian waters. They keep digging and we keep asking, but we only get evasive answers.
The IJC has concluded that the Garrison diversion unit, as envisaged, would have adverse impacts on water uses in Canada. These effects arise primarily from effects on water quantity, water quality and the biological resources of Manitoba. The board has recognized that there are also potential benefits. We do not know what they are. They have not been spelled out. Alterations to the GDU for the purpose of relieving or eliminating some of the impacts are practical. Measures which might be taken in Canada to mitigate impacts may deserve further study. While they are digging, the IJC is telling us we need further studies. This is why I am once again requesting that the Prime Minister make a firm commitment that he will discuss this further with the President of the United States next week.

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) has suggested that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) negotiate with President Carter with a view to placing $50 million in a trust fund to allow for necessary alterations to the project and to establishing a timetable for the work on such alteration.
