NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST THAT MINISTER VISIT EDMONTON TO EXPLAIN RELOCATION OF AIRBORNE REGIMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, originally I addressed this question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) as one member from Edmonton who is very concerned. I expressed grave concern at the sort of non-information and reticence of the minister, and the absolute reticence of the Chief of Defence Staff to discuss the matter of the proposed relocation of the Canadian Airborne Regiment from the Edmonton training area to some split areas in central Canada.
Here I want to speak on behalf of my colleague, the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga), in whose area is located Canadian Forces Base Namao which provides air capability and also the Buxton dropping centre, which is the training area and the Griesbach barracks and ancillary facilities which happen to be presently in Edmonton West, a lot of it going in the future to my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton

Centre (Mr. Paproski), who will be taking over Edmonton North.
All Edmonton area members are vitally concerned. But what raises our hackles is the complete refusal to discuss this matter. Questions have been put to the minister critical of the strategy of denuding the whole of the north west of an active, transportable military force, not clerks, cooks and storemen on the Canadian Forces base. They are not the military presence referred to. We want the whole of the Northwest Territories to be considered.
We have seen fatuous statements made that the unit, or fragments of the unit after it has been broken up, will be transferred to areas where there is a greater concentration of population. That is wrong. Ten years ago, every effort was made by people who considered the Canadian Forces needed an airborne regiment, to bring one into being. There are papers galore on this subject. Those officers, Mr. Speaker, are as highly qualified, then and now, as are General Dextraze and his advisers at the present time.
All I can say, from my point of view and my connections with the Armed Forces, is that General Dextraze is among those who did not agree, years ago, with the formation of the airborne unit, and now that he is in the position of being the chief, his original objection is being implemented by a change which destroys all the work of a succession of commanders of Mobile Command. These are men whose capabilities are as good as those of the officers who are presently there, and they say this is one of the most fatuous moves which could possibly be inflicted upon the forces. If there are reasons, and I presume there are, why is it the minister and the general cannot come clean and tell us what they are? Do not send the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) or the minister in charge of small business (Mr. Marchand) to Edmonton to say the move is justified for military reasons. That is nonsense.
A great deal of money and effort was spent on putting this thing together. I have here a copy of a paper headed "The Selection of a Site for the Canadian Airborne Regiment." This was a working paper utilized in the Armed Forces-

The hon. member's charge of non-information is, of course, without foundation as well, because both the Chief of the Defence Staff and the minister have made several public statements and have made public the rationale for the movement of the airborne regiment from Edmonton.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST THAT MINISTER VISIT EDMONTON TO EXPLAIN RELOCATION OF AIRBORNE REGIMENT
speechtext: They have not given one reason.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST THAT MINISTER VISIT EDMONTON TO EXPLAIN RELOCATION OF AIRBORNE REGIMENT
speechtext:
The hon.
member says they have not. I have before me a statement by General Dextraze to this effect:
At the present moment, I do not believe that the posture of the army field formations in Canada is in balance with military requirements. We have a combat group and an airborne regiment in the west, a small combat group in the centre, and a combat group in Quebec with an independent battalion in the maritimes. This undesirable situation is being redressed by redeploying our land forces in a more balanced posture. The planned overhead savings will be devoted to "The Sharp End" and will allow me to make better use of my total force capabilities.
That is a direct quote from the Chief of the Defence Staff.
Adjournment Debate
The hon. member makes a great deal about the statements made by some retired officers of the Armed Forces. While I will not in any way take away from the service that those people have offered to this country, I will not sit idly by and listen to a dedicated public servant like General Dextraze being attacked in this House where he has no vehicle to defend himself. That is not an honourable course to take in this debate. General Dextraze is an outstanding soldier, an outstanding public servant and an outstanding individual, and is far more competent to judge the needs of the Canadian Armed Forces than some retired generals who happen to have a special interest in the airborne regiment.
That does not mean to say that General Dextraze does not have a special interest in the airborne regiment. But he has the responsibility for redeploying the Armed Forces in Canada to fit the needs of the defence structure of this country. That is his responsibility and the responsibility of the minister. The military forces knew when they joined that they were subject to movement within the country and outside it.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-POSSIBILITY OF RETURN OF MONEY COLLECTED FROM NATIVES THROUGH EXPORT TAX
INDIAN AFFAIRS-POSSIBILITY OF RETURN OF MONEY COLLECTED FROM NATIVES THROUGH EXPORT TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight on the late show I wish to speak again on a question I raised some time ago in December last regarding the possibility of the return of the oil export tax to the Indian people from whose land the oil was extracted. As reported at page 1733 of Hansard for December 7, 1976,1 asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. In regard to the export tax which was collected from Indian bands four years ago, is the minister prepared to state unequivocally that he is going to return the money to the Indian bands, and will he arrange for a tripartite meeting to clear up this whole matter?
I think it is very important. The minister replied that the question is under review. It is important to know that I have been asking the same question now of three successive ministers of Indian affairs and northern development from whom I have received the same answer, namely, that the question is under review and that they will let me know about it.
I have also placed this question on the order paper. I asked how much money has been collected through the export tax from Indian bands, how much is held in the treasury, and, because of the time it is taking the governments to decide what to do in this situation, can the Indian people living on lands where oil is produced expect interest to be paid on this money? Because I have received no answers to this question, I can only assume that the money in question amounts to some $4 million.
We find that a great deal of the money in the Canada Works program is being set aside to provide employment for Indian people because the rate of unemployment among the Indians is the highest in Canada. In many bands it is in the region of 80 per cent or 90 per cent.

February 15, 1977
Adjournment Debate
Surely this money could be put to good use. This is money that rightly belongs to the Indians. They are the ones who should decide what to do with it, how to put it to use to assist members of a band in Finding employment.
Because I was not getting answers from the ministers, I put the question to department officials at a meeting of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development which was held about a month ago. The response of an official, as recorded in the proceedings of the committee, was as follows:
We are actively interested in this and we are looking for a solution that would correspond to the interests expressed by the Indian people of Alberta. I am not fully up to date and I have the impression that some headway is being made as between the province, our department and the Department of Finance ...
I am asking that the federal government provide some leadership and call the provincial government and the bands affected by decision not to return the money, to meet at a tripartite meeting to sort this out once and for all. The Indian people in Alberta should know how much money there is. This is something they do not know for sure. They should also be informed as to whether they can expect any interest on that money which has been collected for four years now.

speakeroldname: Mr. B. Keith Penner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-POSSIBILITY OF RETURN OF MONEY COLLECTED FROM NATIVES THROUGH EXPORT TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) raised this question on December 7 of last year. The question regarding the oil export tax which was collected in respect of oil produced on Indian land and whether this money will be returned to the bands is, of course, a serious and urgent question which has the attention of my minister.
I can say to the hon. member that there is no pat answer. I say that because, as he knows, the question involves three federal departments, the Department of Finance, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I can only speak
for the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and I say to the hon. member that my minister, as well as his two predecessors, the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan), have advanced the requests of the Indian bands concerned that the share of the tax distributed to the provinces should be given to the Indian bands from whose land oil was produced.
As we all know, the Indian people of Canada are unique in that they are the aboriginal inhabitants of the land, and for this reason they deserve special consideration in respect of the reserves of land and minerals set aside for their full use and benefit. In this context, my minister recently wrote letters to his colleagues, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), to see whether a basis can be found to pay over to the Indian bands a share of the tax moneys collected by the federal government under the Oil Export Tax Act. Until their response is in hand, hon. members of this House will appreciate that any unequivocal response such as that sought by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin-and I appreciate his endeavours in seeking this-is just simply not possible from this one minister.
I should make note in addition that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) considers that, again, until the response is received, it would be premature to seek any tripartite meeting to consider the matter.
In conclusion, I appreciate that the hon. member has raised this matter, and I will undertake to add whatever urgency I can to see that we can get an adequate resolution to this serious problem.
